utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The hearing is open. Good morning. I am greeting the OTP and the Defence team. Good morning, Witness. Good morning to all the staff assisting the Court. So good morning, everybody. This morning the Court is going to sit in compliance with Article 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So we're going to proceed with the cross-examination of the Defence witness Mr. Mrkovic, Ljuban Mrkovic, the cross-examination which was started yesterday by Mr. Waespi from the OTP. Now, before we continue with the cross-examination, I would like to read out for the benefit of the parties the new proposals regarding our work programme. It's not going to take very long. The Court suggests that for the rest of the trial that the 20th of August there will be no hearing, contrary to the schedule we had before. So on the 20th of August there will be no hearing. On the 24th of August, we will have the end of the presentation of evidence by the Defence, and at that time we'll also solve a certain number of pending issues regarding this trial. On the 24th of September, we will hear the final briefs. This is what I have in front of me on my paper. So we will have the final submissions. And on the 1st and 2nd of October, we'll have the closing arguments. So, so much for our programme of work, and I'm asking the parties to consult each other and to come back to us in case there are possible objections to that work programme. All right. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, just one sentence, please. A month is not long enough for the Defence to prepare our final brief. Believe me, it is physically impossible for the Defence to prepare the final briefs between the 24th of August and 24th September. We would need at least 10 days more than a month. It's absolutely impossible to even review the material let alone draft our final brief. This is what I had to share with you immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. Well, it's been the practice of this Tribunal to give a one-month time period. Now, I noted what you said, and the Judges are going to consult about this. All right. Now I'll give the floor to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judge Harhoff. Shall I continue cross-examination, or do you want to hear me on the proposed timetable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the proposals of the work programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We have no objections to -- to your proposal, but we understand the suggestion of the Defence, and we would have no objection if you would accede to the Defence proposal to have 10 days more time to prepare the closing briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. Now we're going to continue with the cross-examination. Mr. Waespi, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If document 03285 could be prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think it will take that long this morning. Let me ask you, can you confirm that even in mid-1994, and despite the embargo, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps still received ammunition and, indeed, weaponry from the FRY, from the former Yugoslavia or Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that, because at the time the embargo and the controls on the Drina border were really strict. I crossed the borders very many times, and I could see how strict the controls were. What is the VP 7663, the assistant commander signed. I don't know which military post this is. I can't confirm this because I know that in 1994 and in 1995 we had very little weaponry. We were mostly supplied from the Croatian and the Muslim sides who were selling things to one. I don't know whether there were any secret channels through the forests, meadows, valleys. It is possible, but I'm sure that the prices were very high. There was very little available money, and we could not obtain weapons through any regular routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a look at this document. Apparently, the assistant commander for logistics, Milan Dzurdzic of one of the brigades of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps writes to the SRK, to the command, and it has a reference to a strictly confidential telegram of 26th of June, 1994. And it says the following: "We hereby inform you that we received the following weapons." First point: "From the army of Yugoslavia (according to the approval of the VRS Main Staff) we received the following weapons," and then three different guns. And then it goes on to talking about regular distribution of the SRK. That indeed says that they received -- this unit of the SRK received weaponry from the former Yugoslavia. That's what the document says. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is rather ambiguously drafted. The barracks of the Yugoslavian Han Pijesak and there were some troops that weapons that had not withdrawn. This was the property of the army Yugoslavia and I can't confirm based on this document that this arrived from the army of Yugoslavia. This document was issued by the military post 7673, which I believe was the Vogosca brigade, or maybe even the Rajlovac Brigade. I'm not sure. I'm not sure about the number of the military post. But the property that is referred to here and it was the property of the army of Yugoslavia, just like the engines that were sent to Rajlovac for overhaul and then sent back to the army of Yugoslavia. When there was an embargo on we couldn't do even that; whether this came from some secret channels or some depots, I really can't tell you that. I can only confirm that this is probably an original document which follows the form of our writing, the codes, the type of the dispatches that were sent. And as for the 85-millimetre guns, 40-millimetre guns, I doubt very much that this arrived from the army of Yugoslavia. We had a lot of those guns in the depots in 1994 when the embargo was on and when the United Nations were controlling those borders. It would have been very difficult to transport such things across the Drina or without any controls or checks. It would have been close to impossible, I'd say. I cannot guarantee anything. And the weapons that are indicated here, in my view, it was really not necessary for -- for these weapons to be transported to those areas that are indicated in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the reason for that, that you're saying it was not necessary to have them transported, because you already have these kind of weapons. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say 85-millimetre gun, one piece, without a single shell for that gun, what would that use -- that do without a shell or a rocket launcher without a rocket? And also, you have to have people who are trained to use those pieces. I really don't see a reason for this to be sent to Rajlovac. We did not have an 85-millimetre gun in Rajlovac in the Vogosca Brigade. There may have been two during the war. And as for the shells, if the shells were indicated here in this document, then I would find this document much more credible than the way it is now. During the war in Sarajevo, a signal pistol. I did not -- I did not see a single pistol during the war in Sarajevo and here they're asking for nine pieces. I did not see a single one. Passenger vehicles, we had plenty of those. Now why would the army of Yugoslavia transport passenger vehicles to Rajlovac or Vogosca from some depots. I really don't understand why would that be the case; maybe this was transported from some depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. First of all, you need to slow down a little bit. I know you have a lot to tell to us, but please take it slowly. We have -- we have time. I'm sure you'll get your flight back to -- to the region. But the document --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I didn't get around doing it. I have plenty of time. So if I had not -- if I did not leave yesterday, I can -- I can use all the time you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. But the document is -- is fairly unambiguous. It says that, "We received the following weapons from the army of Yugoslavia," and it doesn't talk about men. It doesn't talk about ammunition. And I suggest to you that there was enough ammunition, and there was enough men to use these weaponry in the SRK. So the only thing they needed was the actual weapons. That's what the document says. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with you at all when you're talking about the staff in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to me as a soldier, at the beginning it numbered some 10.000 men or so, and the highest number it reached, it peaked at 17.500 people. The entire Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the area of responsibility of this corps was -- you see how big it was in this map. The other side, the BiH army, look at all of their reports, the intelligence that we had. It had anything between 70 and 80.000 armed men. Okay, let's put some of that down to propaganda, to boasting, to bragging, to boosting the morale of the people and let's say there were 50.000 of them. According to the military rules if you want to attack, the ratios has to be 1 to 3. In order for us to attack Sarajevo, we would have had to have anything around 150.000 people taking into account the number of armed men in Sarajevo. This is the military doctrine, and that's why there was no moving positions in Sarajevo, very little, if any at all. If we had had enough men, we would have done differently, but here you see the document says that we did not have enough men. If you believe me, I'm sure you -- you can find corroboration in a lot of documents, and you will find that the documents are accurate in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but the document does not talk about men. The document only talks about weaponry coming from the former Yugoslavia. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said it yourself that the document is ambiguous. The document is what it is. I'm looking at it with my own two eyes. But I find it very strange that this was asked from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that this was transported from the army of Yugoslavia. Maybe these things were taken from a depot that was under the control of the VRS. I would find this much more plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the document could be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is being admitted into evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P817, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I didn't get the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 03285, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, you talked yesterday briefly about Marko Lugonja, who was the chief of intelligence and security of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps during the whole period of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you said that you worked with him. Although you were not formally subordinated to him, you had close contact with him during the time you were in -- in Rajlovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was very clear. Down to the professional lines I cooperated with Marko Lugonja. All the intelligence that reached me, that I received since Marko Ljubija was in the territory of responsibility of the Sarajevo Corps was the assistant commander for intelligence. All the intelligence that was relative to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was submitted to Marko Lugonja. That was in compliance with the rules. I was duty-bound to follow the rules. If things did not refer to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I would deliver those things to other units who were interested in those pieces of information. My cooperation with Marko Lugonja lasted throughout the war. At that level he informed me about the things that were necessary for the work of the airport where I worked and for the tasks that I performed at Rajlovac. I'm not trying to escape that. I did cooperate with him, and I did it throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's not an issue I'm concerned about. I wanted to ask you to confirm that Marko Lugonja, at that time a colonel in 1992, was also like you, a professional JNA career officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Marko Lugonja was a colonel, and I was captain, captain first class. A major difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And Colonel Marko Lugonja, he also like other officers made the transition from the 4th JNA Corps right into the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in mid-1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to know this more precisely, he -- Marko Lugonja was serving in Croatia as the intelligence officer in Karlovac when the army withdrew from Croatia, Colonel Lugonja arrived in Sarajevo. He arrived in the command of the 2nd military district and later on the 4th corps, as you call it. And after the army withdrew from Bosnia, he didn't want to do that. He did not want to lose his home again. He remained in Sarajevo, and from the 4th corps -- actually, he withdrew with the army but returned somewhat after -- after me, some two or three months after me. So Marko Lugonja followed that route. He withdrew from Croatia first, then from Bosnia. He went to Belgrade, and from Belgrade he returned to Sarajevo. This is just to clarify the routes that Marko Lugonja followed through -- throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this detailed explanation. In fact, that happened to almost hundred per cent of the JNA commanding officers who were in -- in Sarajevo, at that time, who were from Bosnia. They stayed as well and were transformed into the VRS. The commanding officer, the cadre of the JNA who were from Bosnia, who were part of the JNA, they all transformed into the VRS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give an explanation why that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. Let me just give you an example of the unit that I served in. I claim that 40 per cent of the men in Rajlovac hailed from Bosnia, and they all withdrew to Serbia pursuant to the order of the Supreme Command dated 19th of May. After that, a lot of them who hailed in Bosnia remained in Serbia. Some were necessary for the -- the army. Some didn't want to go back. Some wanted to do other thing -- things. So I can't agree that even 50 per cent of those who hailed from Bosnia and Herzegovina returned and joined the VRS. In my unit, the percentage was under 25 per cent. My institution had 56 officers before the war and a majority of them hailed from Bosnia, and none of them remained in Bosnia. In contrast, we had people who hailed from Serbia who either arrived or remained in 1992, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But everything was done voluntarily. Nobody was forced by anybody else to go somewhere. I went back on -- of my own will. I chose my destiny myself. I chose myself to go back to Bosnia and to do what I did. So I really cannot accept your hundred per cent claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Marko Lugonja gave an interview to the Office of the Prosecutor in -- on the 19th November 2000, and he was asked whether -- that's on page 6 of -- of an interview that has been disclosed, of course, to the Defence. He was asked whether the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, Your Honours. I apologise to my learned friend Mr. Waespi, but I have not received that document. I looked through the documents carefully, but I don't think I received it. Perhaps I have overlooked something, but I don't think. I don't think I have received the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have this issue before. I don't intend to tender this document as an exhibit. It's merely to put propositions from what other witnesses, potential witnesses, real witnesses said to the OTP, and that's possible in -- in cross-examination. I do have two hard copies with me of the interviews which were disclosed some time ago. If the Defence wants to have it, I'm happy to hand it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But did you send it to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President, as part of our disclosure because it's highly relevant for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you remember when you disclosed it to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe a year ago, two years ago. We can certainly check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was not put on the list. I have received millions of pages, but it wasn't on the list, nor is it on the list now. Had I been informed, I have certainly studied -- I would have certainly studied it carefully. Now, if it was sent out two years ago, well, I have no supernatural powers, and I apologise to my colleague Mr. Waespi, but if he had at least told me of this yesterday then I would have taken it on board. Now, two years ago -- well, I can't look into a crystal ball and say what is going to be used in this trial through certain witnesses. I have to know this at least a day in advance, or that it should be disclosed after the witness takes the solemn declaration when he starts his testimony, and that wasn't done either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can give an explanation; I tried beforehand. We had issue about whether documents or exhibits, potential exhibits, need to be disclosed as part of the list of exhibits or documents which we intend to use, and I have used this document, this interview before. I think it was Witness Veljovic, the first Defence witness. And it was decided that, if I do not intend to exhibit a document, if I do not intend to propose the document I'm quoting from as an exhibit, there is no need nor duty to inform the Defence beforehand. That was the practice I believe that was accepted by Your Honours. So -- but out of convenience for the Defence, I do have a copy of the document here, a hard copy, even in B/C/S, which I'm happy to give to the Defence, and they can look perhaps at the context of it. But there is no duty from my side to indicate which document, which newspaper article, whatever, I'm putting to the witness, if I have no intention to have it admitted as an exhibit. That's my understanding, Mr. President. And the document was disclosed on the 21st of June, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Tapuskovic, I think that we all agree. The OTP disclosed the document to you, among many documents, two years ago, in 2005, and now we are in the context of the cross-examination following on the examination-in-chief yesterday; and therefore, the Prosecutor, having to deal with the questions that you yourself addressed to the witness, is entitled to use the document that is on the list of documents that were submitted to you. This is consistent with the practice of the Trial Chamber. And therefore, I allow him to use this document, knowing that it will not be admitted into evidence or tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I consider that it is quite contrary to the rules of this Tribunal. A few days ago we had a witness. It was Witness T-27. And we had a discussion about that, and I can't understand the fact -- it was Witness Kovacevic, in actual fact. And there was a whole piece of the transcript that was going to be put to the witness. But in principle, if something is not on the list of documents that will be used, then cannot be used. The fact that we were disclosed something two years ago is immaterial in this kind of situation when we have before us a witness. We must be provided with the documents that are going to be used and put to the witness. Otherwise, I'm going to have to ask for more time to study the documents, and once I've done that to accept or -- or not having the witness examined on the documents. So I object, but you can decide. I'm waiting for your ruling. If you make a ruling to the contrary, then I will accept that, but it is quite contrary to what we discussed with respect to Witness T-27 a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I do not believe that the case of Witness T-27 is identical. At any rate, the Trial Chamber has already ruled, and so what you have said does not change this in any way. Mr. Waespi, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I offer a hard copy of this interview in English and B/C/S for the Defence if they want to have it. It's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mrkovic, when we interviewed Mr. Lugonja, and this is on page 6 of both the English and the B/C/S version, he was asked by the investigator, Mr. Barry Hogan, when the 4th Corps returned to Yugoslavia on 19th May, did they take all their men and all their equipment with them?" Mr. Lugonja answered "No." Then Mr. Hogan: "Is that the essential part which actually became the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the men and the equipment that stayed behind the 4th Corps?" The answer was: "Commanding officers within the 4th Corps who were from Bosnia, who were born in Bosnia stayed and they were -- maybe, I think 95 per cent of them, stayed." That's what Marko Lugonja told us. 95 per cent of all the officers of the 4th Corps who were from Bosnia, they stayed behind and were transformed into the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Do you accept what the chief of intelligence of the SRK said to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Marko Lugonja said that, then he probably had reason for saying that. And he knows about things like that. I'm talking about Rajlovac and the unit that I was in. That's what I'm talking about. I really don't know what the composition of the 4th Corps was or the command of the 2nd Military District. I know that they had a precipitous increase of men with the withdrawal of the army from Zagreb. That's what I do know. But what the percentage was, now 95 per cent, I don't know. Where were these officers during the war? Because if you have a brigade, for example, the 1st brigade, 2nd, 3rd Brigade, the commanders of battalions and so on, where are the officers then if you have 95 per cent of those officers staying on from the 4th Corps, which means that we would have an active officer commander in each brigade or battalion. And at Ilidza in the brigade command, we only had one active commander who held the rank of an ordinary captain. I don't know where they were hiding or hidden from us. I don't doubt the figures. Perhaps they are exact ones. They might have just left and dispersed. But I'm talking about the Rajlovac Brigade where the commander was an ordinary captain. The commanders of the battalions had secondary school training. Perhaps one of them or some of them had trained at the reserve officers school. Now, I do believe what Marko Lugonja said, but I'm wondering where were those people then. And if you look at the composition of any brigade, you'll see that the situation was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Mrkovic is speaking very fast. He'd have to speak slower, because it's too fast for the record. I don't know whether the record will reflect all this. I don't know whether this will be done, but whole sentences have been left out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, please be reminded that the interpreters need to be able to follow you, so please speak more slowly. But I wanted to ask the Prosecution, since we have spent some time on this issue as to how the SRK was composed, what is -- what is your argument? What is your point in bringing this up? What is it that you want the Chamber to extract from -- from this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that goes again to background of what happened in 1992. Paragraph 7 of the indictment, which talks about a transformation, transition of the JNA units that supposedly left because they were told to do so by the Security Council, but leaving behind much of its equipment and, indeed, cadre, as we heard, transforming into the SRK. So this was a gradual process which happened at that time and which explains, in our submission, the situation that evolved starting from 1992, throughout the conflict until November 1995. So it is more background for Your Honours to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I -- thank you. I understand. But what difference would it make if the officers were born in Bosnia and Sarajevo rather than being people from somewhere else in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Probably not much difference, but people were born from Sarajevo. They knew Sarajevo, and they were familiar with the weaponry, with the surroundings, with the advantage points. And, indeed, they were familiar with their enemies as it were, and we'll come to that in a moment. These were people who were from Sarajevo and were fighting people who were also from Sarajevo. That's a different -- a difference to when somebody else comes in, somebody else fresh who has nothing to do with the situation in Sarajevo. That's part of what the Prosecution says happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next point, Mr. Mrkovic, I wanted to ask you about, if you have any knowledge, is the issue of snipers or sharpshooters. Yesterday, you told us that your institute in Rajlovac was attacked by infantry weapons, including snipers. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these snipers were part of which army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But the SRK had also snipers, is that correct, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a single army without any snipers? There is not. Within the establishment of any military unit, infantry unit, I'm talking about the infantry units now, they all have snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. So we can move on to the next issue, the last one connected to Marko Lugonja. He was asked about the general nature of the conflict in -- in Sarajevo, and he described it as a civil war. And he said the following, I'd like you to listen carefully to what I'm putting to you, and for the Defence benefit it's on page 50, in the English version and on page 51, in the B/C/S version. Marko Lugonja says the following, Mr. Mrkovic: "I have another thing to say. Civil war on religious and national basis, Yugoslavia was the only country in Europe in which three big world religions were distributed equally --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another comment with respect to what we said at the beginning. If that is the case, if all this that we haven't read yesterday and today, then we'd like to see Marko Lugonja here to cross-examine him, because I don't think we can proceed in this manner. I see no danger here for the accused Dragomir Milosevic, but in principle, it is the same problem that we had with the other witness a few days ago. So this voluminous statement pulled out of context, and there are dozens of pages, 110 pages, to be exact, we -- this would have to be something that could be tested through the cross-examination of this witness -- of a witness, if he were a Prosecution witness. Otherwise, I don't understand where this is leading with all due respect to my colleague Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the -- the Chamber believes that there's a huge difference between admitting a document into evidence and -- on the one hand, and on the other hand, to confront a witness with documents on which the only thing you wish to have is the witness's comments to what is in that document. And I fully agree with you that if the issue is that a certain document is brought up in the courtroom for the purpose of tendering it into evidence, and if that document is a statement that is taken from a witness, from another witness, then I agree in that case we should certainly allow the Defence to have that witness come into the courtroom for cross-examination. That goes without saying. But I think that there is a difference between this situation on the one hand and the other hand where you are just confronting the witness that we have in front of us for the purpose of getting his comments and nothing else. Do you accept this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I do understand what you've just said, Judge Harhoff. However, even when these things are put, I think that this statement, this testimony, is and lengthy one which requires careful examination for one to understand the whole context of it. And then having grasped the context, I would be able to address every question put by the Prosecutor given the entire context of the material, and that is why I think that the Defence is at a disadvantage, whether this is tendered and admitted or not, because if you extract fragments, then it doesn't show you the whole picture. And if I were to study this carefully, who knows what I would find in addition to these sentences that are used as a trigger for the examination. So that is my line of thinking and why I raised the objection. Otherwise, I understand the fate of this document, because in my opinion it can, of course, not be admitted into evidence. I understand what you're saying, and I can't go against that, but I can present my own views. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But rest assured, Mr. Tapuskovic, that the Chamber will have no interest in the earlier statement which you have now received by the earlier witness. We're only interested in this witness's comments, and this is the only thing at that we will take into consideration for the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi, you may pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, I totally agree what I'm reading out is not evidence in itself. Evidence is whether the witness accepts it or not. And it's also a fair comment by the Defence saying that it shouldn't -- issues that are put to the witness shouldn't be taken out of context, and I try not to do that. That's why I'm reading a whole part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, Witness, let me go back to what Marko Lugonja told us in November 2000. He said that: "Yugoslavia was the only country in Europe in which three big world religions were distributed equally, Catholics, Orthodox, and Muslim. But the problem was that national and religious aspects were always connected or tied up. And on this territory, all the wars -- most of the wars were on the same basis, were waged on the same basis. For example, during the war you had commander Delic on one front line who was Orthodox, and there was Muslim Commander Delic. They both speak the same language. Until yesterday they went to the same cafe to drink together, and somehow they managed to -- the idea of killing each other in their heads. And you have the same situation in Sarajevo as well. People who knew each other so well, and maybe all lived in the same building, fired at each other. And there is not much mercy there. It's worse than, say, if the Austrian army came in." And the last paragraph: "Because it's historical memory, memory of history, their grandfathers and grand-grandfathers waged the same wars and the everyone thinks that he has got molested worse than the other side, and he needs to make up for it in this war. So the hatred is almighty motive that is produced so quickly in such conditions." Now, do you share the assessment of Marko Lugonja of what he perceived from his sources being throughout the war in Sarajevo as the chief of intelligence and security? Do you share his assessment of the causes and the way the war was waged in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I can say that I agree in part with the statement, that it was a national war or ethnic war, part of Croatia and so on. There I would agree with his evaluation. But I wouldn't agree with one of the things that was stated. We came to Sarajevo, lived for a few months in Sarajevo, and then say how the war came about. The war in Sarajevo was probably being prepared far in advance by those who intended to wage it. Marko Lugonja arrived in Sarajevo only in 1991, and the war could not be organised in five minutes or five months. It could not come about during that short space of time. The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please do not forget to speak more slowly to allow the interpreters and court reporters to follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you like to continue, or is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at the wars in 1941, 1939 on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Look at that war and then you'll see. And as Prosecutor of this Tribunal, take a look at history, the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We would need a lot of time to talk about what happened there at that time or during the last century. And it is within that context that we can then speak about what the war in Sarajevo is. That it was a national war, I do agree there. That I drank coffee with my Muslim colleagues, that's true. We would greet each other, kiss each other in parting, and we would each go our different ways. I cry when my colleague is killed, and the Muslims cry when one of us is killed. So that was the war in Sarajevo as we experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, because you said that some parts you accept, some you don't. I think the key of what Marko Lugonja says is his last sentence; where he says that"hatred is almighty motive that is produced so quickly in such conditions." Would you agree that hatred was part of the way war was waged in Sarajevo between the two warring factions? Would you were with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have nothing against the witness presenting his own views, and I am quite certain that he could tell us a lot more, things that could be to the Defence's advantage, but to ask the witness about all this, and his opinion -- to compare his opinion to somebody else's opinion, well, I don't mind listening to Mrkovic further, and I'm sure he could tell you a great many more things about who cried for who and what kind of war that was, but that was not something that a witness needs to tell us here. At least that is my opinion. He's a witness here who is here to tell us what he himself saw in Rajlovac and the surrounding parts, in the geographical area that he lived in. But of course if you want to hear other things from him, I don't mind. And you'll hear of all the suffering that lead up to the conflict. But I think that is up to you to assess, but otherwise those views I don't think serve any purpose at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed I do wonder, because do you think you can really did the witness whether hatred was one of the causes of this war as Mr. Marko Lugonja asserted? What exactly is the foundation of this kind of question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's less the causes than what happened during the war. And the witness was a very senior intelligence security officer in Sarajevo. Perhaps limited to Rajlovac, but he was also at the airport. And based on his information he gathered, I'm just interested what he thinks are, you know, the ways soldiers waged -- waged war. What their motives were and I -- I'd like to hear his view also in contrast to what the chief of intelligence of the SRK said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi, the Trial Chamber would like you to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be allowed to say just one more sentence in response to the Prosecutor's question about hatred?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to Defence Exhibit 307, which was discussed by the Defence with you yesterday. If that could be retrieved, please. You remember that document was an ABiH document that discussed the preparations of the SRK in anticipation of the breakout of the ABiH. Do you remember discussing this document with the Defence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the assessment or the basis, the sources for the assessment of the ABiH included comments from, and I quote it on English page 2, line 5, and it's on page 1 of the Serbian version where it starts, "Iz komentara." "The basis for the assessment of the ABiH was comments of stated aggressors officers." So that means that the ABiH somehow talked to SRK officers or at least had access to some information from the other side. Is that true? At least as it relates to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the exact place where this is stated, where this is indicated? Can the witness please be allowed to read that place first before he's allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Could you tell us where exactly this is written?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's about the eighth line from the bottom of the first page of the B/C/S version it starts "Iz komentara."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the comments" -- "From the comments of the BiH army" -- no it's not here. I don't know what you wanted to say by this from the comments. "From the comments of the aforementioned aggressor officers, it is obvious they are privy to information." Is that what you're referring to, but the sense is completely different. It says here, "from the comments." Please read, and I will also take another moment to read the whole thing. "From the comments of the aforementioned aggressor officer, it is clear that they are privy to the information that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina --" would you like me to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure they were also engaged in intelligence as we did, and that from our comments maybe they were eavesdropping on our officers and our telephone conversations. We did the same. Maybe we learned that we were aware of the fact that they were preparing for an offensive. It was our right to prepare for a counter-attack. And I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was good that we both knew what the other side was doing, because if everybody knew everything, then it was easy to find a common language.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I was about to -- to base my question on, that you knew from information what the other side was -- was doing. Now let me go to the last --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, no, not all. Nobody is saying that we knew all. We received information, some of which was false. I didn't say that we knew everything, that we knew everything to the last letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the last sentence of this document, and you were asked about that by the Defence yesterday. And it says here, and it's the last sentence in B/C/S as well, I'll read it in English at the end of page 2: "Based on this and previous knowledge, we are of the opinion that Serbian terrorists shall, by using artillery missiles of great destructive power, act in the following days upon the City of Sarajevo and nearby and at the same time try the certain offensive actions, most probably in the direction of Ilidza." So that's the assessment of the ABiH of what could be happening in the next few days from the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what they wrote. Whether this is correct or not is an entirely different matter. I'm just commenting on what it says in the document. There is no document without the last sentence being appended to it. Here they call us Chetniks, Serb aggressor. I was not an aggressor. I was living in my territory. And I'm insulted by that derogatory terms. Would you agree with that, that I was not an aggressor of any sort, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think it's my job to comment on at that. Let me ask you if you have any knowledge about --

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are the one who have read it out to me. There is no document - this is what I was saying - in which they did not add at the end that we would be shelling Sarajevo, that the Serb army would be shelling Sarajevo. That's probably also the reason why they could later on plant an explosion here and there when they found it convenient in political and military terms. They would kill somebody in Sarajevo. For example, in Djurodjapkovic [phoen], five Serbs were killed there in 1993. I don't know the date. Yesterday, you asked me about the investigations. Sniper bullets from the Serbian police -- Serbian positions could not reach Djurodjapovica [phoen] Street. There were such cases also, but we could go on for five days talking about things like that. But this was a sentence that was a staple sentence in every document, especially their state intelligence that was headed by Enver Mujezinovic who was a good mate of mine from before the war and he was succeeded by Ugljen. He continued along the same course and that was the last staple sentence that was appended to all their reports, without a single shell having fallen anywhere before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi, according to the calculations of the registrar you already used up an hour and 45 minutes for your cross-examination which was only to last two hours, which means that you have 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I will certainly comply, be within that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you about if you know the word artillery missiles of great destructive power which is mentioned in here. Do you have any idea what the ABiH intelligence might be referring to? Could that be air bombs perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, a mortar shell, 60-millimetre, is also destructive and a great missile, not to go any further. Those also have great destructive power, those mortars shells. A 60-millimetre mortar shell wreaks havoc among the troops, among the civilian population. So I don't have to go any further to explain why this is a great destructive power. Let's not even -- let's not even talk about a 250 kilogramme bomb. That is also huge destructive power.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I could not agree more with you about that. But the SRK did have air bombs. You mentioned 250-kilogramme bombs, that was in the possession of the SRK and they used it. Did you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Hold on just a second. Who said that the SRK had air -- air bombs? I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps air bombs, I didn't say that. You're putting this to me and I never said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you, did the SRK have air bombs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the air bombs that we had remained in the depot in Busovaca for the entire former Yugoslavia. Everything was in the depot in Busovaca. When you're talking about the air bombs in the SRK, I did hear some information about those air bombs, but as far as I know, there were very few, if any at all, in the units. Why they were requested, why they -- you saw document that Haris Silajdzic and Alija Izetbegovic brought 800 air bombs, but I don't know why. They didn't have any aircraft. In Banja Luka there were aircraft but they couldn't fly over. So I don't know why the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina should have requested air bombs if they didn't have aeroplanes. You know very well what an air bomb is. You have to an aeroplanes to be able to use air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm talking about SRK, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I'm talking about air bombs which were modified to fire them from makeshift launchers in the area of responsibility of the SRK or from the area of responsibility of the SRK. Do you have any knowledge of them using air bombs, modified air bombs including these 250 kilos you mentioned? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about my information, I can share with you my view that I held at that time. There was talk about those air bombs. I didn't see anything personally or hear anything personally. I only heard from other sources. My personal position is always -- has always been that an air bomb can only be used by throwing it from an aeroplane. There is no genius who can come up with a launchpad for this bomb to be launched from it. But those were not soldiers who speculated about that or did that. Those were some poorly organised groups who only had their thought in their heads. I also heard information that never reached me through official channels that a group did try to do that, that somebody was killed in the course of doing that through unprofessional handling. I don't know whether the attempt was abandoned quickly or not, but let me tell you I know what an air bomb is, how it's attached to an aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness -- if Prosecution Exhibits P225, could be retrieved, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we leave --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll stay on the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you going to change the document? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- I have a question and that's why I'm intervening. So before we leave this Exhibit D307, I would like to put a few questions to the witness because I'm not sure that I have fully understood the meaning of this document. As far as I can see, it's a letter from the ABiH commander Hadzihasanovic, in which he speaks about intelligence that he has received about the knowledge that the SRK had about the forthcoming and planned attacks of the ABiH to break out of Sarajevo. That is to say, that the ABiH commander knew that the SRK was aware of the ABiH plans to launch an attack, and also that the ABiH commander knew that the SRK, on its side, had prepared a counter-attack. Is that correctly understood? And if I am right in assuming this, then my question is, what sort -- or do you know what sort of counter-attack the SRK had planned? So these are two questions. Firstly, if you could advise me if I have understood this correctly, and then if that is so, what were the counter-attacks the SRK had in mind, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put it this way: You have understood the document well, but let me just draw your attention to one thing. Let's go back to the first page of that document. This is not Rasim's document, the document of the commander of the main staff, this is a document by the chief of the state security of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was sent to President Izetbegovic to Rasim Delic, the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the MUP minister. Bakrac Alispahic who was the minister of the interior is superior to the person who drafted this document and this document was only forwarded to Rasim Delic, the commander of the army and that was their task, official task. They had to inform of their intentions every -- of these addressees. This is the only main difference. Otherwise, you have understood the document well. This is not Rasim Delic's document. This is a document by the state security services that forwarded the document to all those who were interested in the -- as for the intention, of course that the document exaggerates the work of the intelligence service, portraying them as knowing everything and being able to do everything. I would only be able to laugh at that. We all very often laugh at things. The intention of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at the time was defence and nothing but defence operations. Defence, defence, defence. At least in the area of responsibility where I was, but I believe that the same went on in -- in the other parts of the Sarajevo region. I'm talking about defence and nothing but defence. In -- in that offensive, we were really on the defensive, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I do understand you, and I accept, of course, that a counter-attack is a perfectly legitimate attack in anticipation of -- of attack from the other side. But my question was really, if indeed the SRK did plan some sort of counter-attacks, do you then know what these counter-attacks were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the corps command planned is nothing I can talk about. I did not receive this document. However, in the -- in the area of Rajlovac we were not planning any counter-attacks. All we did was defending ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to finish off this, Prosecution Exhibit 225, please. This document you are about to see is a combat report from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and it goes up to the Main Staff of the VRS, it dates of 7 April 1995. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you can see that on page 2, of the Serbian version and also on the page 2 of the English version, you have, "Our forces." The second paragraph. Can you see that? Mr. Mrkovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll read it out, it says: "We responded to enemy fire as follows: "In Ilidza by infantry arms, PA gun and 82 millimetre BST. "In Ilidza, infantry brigade one 120-millimetre mine was fired and one 250-kilogramme AB was launched at the centre of Hrasnica. According to the interception centre, the Muslims claim that the Luna rocket landed. "In the 2nd Slpbr, we responded to enemy attacks by infantry weapons 60, 82, and 100-millimetre MB." That states by the commander of the SRK and not by some soldiers who speculated about doing it, as you put it, that indeed a 250-kilogramme air bomb was launched at the centre of Hrasnica. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it. I didn't hear it. If the document is original, then -- but to launch an air bomb from any launchpad my -- my opinion, the opinion of a person who knows what an air bomb is, I wouldn't dare do it, and I would not dare order anybody else to do it. A 250 air bomb, if that bomb had exploded in Hrasnica, half Hrasnica would be missing if such a bomb had fallen on it. I spent a lot of time in tactical firing from the aeroplane with these bombs, napalm bombs. I believe half of Hrasnica would be missing. There was a lot of exaggeration for psychological effect on both sides. I really wouldn't comment upon this document if this document is what it is and if it is original. If I were commander, I would never allow this. It would never even occur to me that somebody would be able to do that. I'm not talking about only about 250-kilogramme bombs but to improvise a launchpad on the ground and to launch a bomb from it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Waespi, the Prosecution. Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yesterday, my examination-in-chief was somewhat shorter, but today I would have a few things to discuss. I would like to go back to D307. Can this be shown to the witness once again please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I read out the sentence, I don't want to go into that again because Mr. Mrkovic is having a hard time reading it. I would like to read that sentence again, the sentence at the end. But before that let's start from, first things first, and that is the date of the document which was drafted by the assistant minister of the SDB or the state security services. What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26 August 1995. Immediately before the events that took place at Markale, maybe two or three days before that. I was going to draw the Prosecutor's attention to that, but he went very fast through it. This is a very, a very important document, and the last sentence in it indicated that something would be happening, some air bombs, heavy artillery. Things like that would been -- in preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had had this document on the 26th of August, this document would have told me that we would be surprised by something like we were always surprised by something at the strategic or tactical level. This was a strategic level -- level which should have been expected since Izetbegovic and the state security were involved. We could have assessed in advance what would happen if we had had this document at the time, which we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Now I'm a bit clearer on things. Before becoming the assistant minister, yesterday you saw who signed this, Nedzad Ugljen, that was, did he belong to an organisation of some sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The witness was asked in chief about this gentleman already and he explained what he had to say. I didn't touch on it in cross-examination. I don't see how that arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, so what do you think about this objection raised by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua, with all due respect, the Prosecutor dealt with this document in his cross-examination. I would like to seek additional clarification because Judge Harhoff also asked him something and I would like us to clarify what this document announced, what it was announcing, with your permission of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's giving you leave for this because Judge Harhoff did indeed put a question on this matter. Please do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you have this document, and once you've seen it, in view of what happened on the 28th, what about did this document in fact announce?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- I'm really sorry. The issue that Judge Harhoff raised a specific point certainly allows the Defence to go into that point, having it clarified, and also if I, in cross-examination raise an issue, that's fine, but to go back -- in fact, to talk about Markale, I did not talk about Markale, what happened on the 28th of August. All that was raised in chief already, and neither did Judge Harhoff talk about the events of the 28th. That's a huge issue, and I have not touched it because the basis of the witness is very, very thin. So I really object of the Defence, just because this document was on the screen, on the table, to go over it again. I think his re-examination, despite the fact that he might have cut his examination-in-chief short yesterday, his re-examination has to be focused on issues that were raised in cross-examination or questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, there is some merit in what the Prosecution brings up, but I think, nevertheless, that if you wish to put a question to the witness as to whether the Markale incident, which followed two days after this document, whether the Markale incident was one of the counter-attacks that were contemplated in the SRK, then I would be interested in hearing the witness's answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not receiving the interpretation. There's something wrong with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the matter, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript isn't working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We're going to take the break now and we're going to sort out the technical problem. So we're going to resume in 20 minutes' time. The hearing is suspended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkovic, in view of the questions you were asked by His Honour Judge Harhoff and the topic we were discussing with respect to the document, since you've already said that the document was compiled on the 25th of August, 1995, and in view of the question you were asked by Judge Harhoff about whether the document speaks of a counter-offensive being prepared by the army of Republika Srpska, I am forced, Your Honours, to read out the last sentence; and then the witness can answer and tell us what in fact this document, in his view, once he has read it, states. Are we dealing here with an intimation, an announcement of counter-offensive operation by the BH army or is it a question of all we've said so far, the information you had in view of the date recorded and in fact, what this was about, what it meant based on the information you already had during that time and in view of what happened later?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document, I did not understand it that the army of Republika Srpska was preparing a counter-attack or any other type of attack. All I can understand from this document, having read it carefully, and if you read it carefully, is that the BH army -- in fact, the state security sent in a document to the BH army to the effect that the army of Republika Srpska had at its disposal information about its offensive and that the offensive would take place in the next two days, that we should be aware of that, and they were preparing for this shelling of Sarajevo. And as I said, in the latest report that sentence always existed. There was always that sentence. The document itself indicates the fact that they'd already written in advance that Sarajevo would be shelled and that they probably knew where it would happen. But on the basis of this document we can understand that the shelling of Sarajevo was imminent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that, then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th, as we well know, Markale happened. I don't wish to talk about Markale here because I am not competent to do so, but that Markale happened, yes, they did. And I leave it up to the experts to determine the method and way in which the shell fell. Whether it fell or it was planted or whatever, I leave that up to the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But was this an announcement that that would happen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, we did not think that something major like that would happen but that things were planted before, I can say that with full responsibility before this Court, but we didn't actually know that it would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you can't tell us now either who Nedzad Ugljen was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues who worked on the same things that I worked on I don't want to talk about. I would have a lot to say but, of course, he's a colleague of mine, and he could say a lot of things about me. So what I heard and saw and experienced was not perhaps correct, and I don't want to speak in this courtroom about Nedzad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just a few more points. You mentioned the air bombs in response to a question from the Prosecution. Now, what you know about air bombs in general, what is that? You had occasion to see them in action, did you? But tell us, how are air bombs manipulated? How are they used, deployed? When it comes to the installation of an air bomb on a plane, how does that -- how does one go about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The handling of an air bomb is a subject that is the -- of a very thick book written, which is a very voluminous work, over 120 pages long. It -- and aeronautical technicians who handle this type of bomb, to place one bomb on an air wing would require 10 people. You need the launching pad. You need to bring the bomb out of the depot, place it on the movable -- the -- the vehicle to take it to the aeroplane. So it's a great science. And it's only experts that can handle things like that. And I told you what the destructive power of air bombs was a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's precisely what I wanted to ask you. If an air bomb were to fall anywhere, be dropped anywhere, what does it release? What is the impact if we take a 250-kilogramme air bomb; for example, and all the features of that kind, a bomb. I don't want to ask any leading questions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pressure created by an air bomb is such that within a radius of 150 metres nothing would remain standing. People would be killed and the destructive power of its shrapnels is enormous. And if an air bomb were to fall on Sokolovic, at least a third of the Sokolovic colony would have been destroyed and the victims would be innumerable. And as I know there were a lot of -- it was a densely populated settlement. A third of it would have been destroyed with a great deal of human casualty involved. .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could an air bomb of such destructive power explode with just two, three, or not a single shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't have an air bomb with just two or three shrapnels. If you have another type of air bomb, the M-72 hand bomb, and we call it a fort bomb, if you have five or six balls in one, and in another with 500 shrapnels in this small bomb that is a hand launched bomb, it's a hand grenade, actually, well, you can calculate the destructive power for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, just one more question. In response to a question from my learned friend Mr. Waespi, you spoke about snipers and said that you wouldn't find a single army in the world without a sniper, without snipers in it. Now, the armies -- as armies have to have snipers, tell us what these snipers are used for.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are rules and regulations about the deployment of snipers. If you have a sniper nest somewhere, then you would attack that sniper nest by using a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I wish to put a few questions to you to clarify your answer to the questions by Counsel Tapuskovic. My question relates again to the interpretation of documents Delta 307, and I'm now quoting from your answer, and I'm putting the question to you because I'm not sure I fully understand what it was you really said. And if I read from the transcript, you said that the army of Republika Srpska, this is on page 38, line number 3. That: "Army of Republika Srpska had at its disposal information about its offensive and that the offensive would take place in the next two days, that we should be aware of that, and they were preparing for the shelling of Sarajevo. "And as I said in the latest report that sentence always existed. There was always that sentence. The document itself indicates the fact that they'd already written in advance that Sarajevo would be shelled and that they probably knew where it would happen, but on the basis of this document, we can understand that the shelling of Sarajevo was imminent." This is what you said. End of quotation. What I'm not sure about is who are you referring to when you say that the shelling of Sarajevo was imminent? I -- I think what you're saying here is that the SRK had planned shelling of Sarajevo as a defensive measure taken in anticipation of the -- of the attack that they knew was coming from the ABiH. So I would like you to confirm if that is what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I don't have the right to object to the Court's questions, but that's not what it says in the transcript. He said he does not understand -- I did not understand this assertion. It's -- that's what it says, Judge Harhoff, if we look at the transcript on page 37, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting me in my interpretation of the witness's answer. I am fully aware of the opening remark, and I understand this opening remark as the witness's immediate interpretation of what the document says. My question, nevertheless, relates to what was the witness's knowledge about the counter-attacks that the SRK apparently had planned. Mr. Tapuskovic, the interest I have in this issue is to find out what were the counter -- the defensive -- what were the legitimate defensive counter-measures which the SRK had planned in anticipation of the ABiH attack, and -- and my question goes to the witness if he had any knowledge of these counter-attacks on the basis of the suggestion made in the document that such counter-attacks were indeed planned. So there you have it. And I still need to hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand this document in the following way: That the BH army is being informed that the army of Republika Srpska knows about the -- their intentions for an offensive. It learnt about their intentions for an offensive, and that's normal. And they are issuing a warning now. They are saying that we know about it, and in the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's written wrongly again on the transcript, Judge Harhoff, and that might lead you astray. "Of their offensive." The witness said "their offensive." Here it says "an offensive." That's a big difference and that can lead you astray when you read. It can be corrected later on, of course, but there's no value in that. It's their offensive, not an offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I have been quoting from the transcript, and I would like the witness to give his reply, and then if you have remarks to make about possible mistakes in the interpretation, then you can do so, but let the witness finish now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood the document in the following way: That the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is being informed by the state security that the army of Republika Srpska knows about their intentions for an offensive and that the army of Republika Srpska is preparing for that attack of theirs. The Rajlovac area responsibility of the army of Republika Srpska and where I was also received a piece of information. I remember that very well when I think back now about the intentions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to carry out an attack along all axes, especially along the Ilidza axis, and quite normally we were preparing for that attack. And we didn't have a single order to launch a counter-offensive. So the exclusive intention at least in the area of responsibility where I was, was defence. And we used all our engineering -- we carried out all our engineering work within the space of 48 hours and there were no further attacks. Now, what you're asking me about, I don't think you will find a single order of ours where somebody ordered or wrote that the town, the city, should be shelled as a town. Now, to shell positions, that is the legitimate right of each army in defence. As to a town that I knew that somebody had the intention of doing this to a town, nobody did in an offensive of that kind where they're being prepare -- where they are preparing, we did not have the intention of shelling the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. I understand you to say that the suggestion made in this letter about knowledge inside the ABiH that the SRK had planned counter-attacks must be wrong. The -- the SRK did not plan, to your knowledge, any such counter-attacks. And so if the ABiH had information about or intelligence about such counter-attacks, then that counter-intelligence is wrong. That is how I understand your testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBAN MRKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any objections against this Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have some comments and I objected to the transcript. When the transcript comes up before you, it could lead you astray. You might not be properly informed about his answer while he was answering. But I have no objections to your questions, of course, neither will I ever make any objections to your questions. And the witness has already answered, and he's given you an answer again to your question, and I have no comments or objections to make there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Prosecution, do you have any comments to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, fine. I think that we're coming now to the end of this witness's testimony. Turning to the witness, I would like to thank you very much, sir. The Chamber thanks you for coming over to The Hague to bring your contribution to international justice. I would like to wish you a safe journey back home and a lot of success in your endeavours. You're now being released and you can leave the room. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the next witness is Witness T-21. His name and surname is Momcilo Gojkovic. And there are no protective measures requested for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I understand that the witness has no protection measures. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. I think the usher is going to introduce the witness any minute now. All right. For this witness we are going to devote an hour and 30 minutes for the Defence and an hour 30 minutes for the Prosecution. So we're going to try to stick to the speaking time, because we will still have other witnesses to hear today. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have two more witnesses today, the one that is just coming into the courtroom and one more, and we hope to conclude with those witnesses perhaps even before the end of business today. Another witness that was to have come in has, unfortunately, been taken ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So among the remaining two or one of these two. Who is sick, one of these two or another one? So we have the witness who is here, but then there are two more; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This one and T-15 with protective measures. This witness will have three hours, the second one, two hours. And the witness which was supposed to have also come in has broken his leg and is not here at all, but he will come in at some point perhaps, and I'll try and be as rational with my use of time as possible. But I think that these two witnesses that we have planned for today will finish in the course of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you very much for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. The Chamber thanks you for coming over to The Hague to make your testimony. I would like you to stand up, please, and tell me if you can understand in your own language what I am telling you. If that is the case, tell me yes, and I will understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. I will ask the registrar to make sure that you're reading out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please do sit down now. Pursuant to the practice of this Chamber, I'm going to ask the Defence counsel, and ask Mr. Tapuskovic representing the Defence today, to check your identity, and then we are going to have the examination-in-chief. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will do as you ask.
