utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you please tell the Judges your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Momcilo Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were born on the 26th of September, 1951?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please wait for the entire text to be typed out and then when the cursor stops then you can begin your answers, regardless of how short the questions are. You were born in Sarajevo, in Novo Sarajevo? That's a Sarajevo municipality, in the Stanojevici neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again you didn't wait for the text to finish, and again there could have been a problem. So, I ask you please pay attention to this. We will not get very far if you do not wait for the end of the question and for it to be completely typed into the transcript. You finished elementary school in the settlement or neighbourhood of Vraca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you finished secondary electrical engineering school in Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you completed your regular term of duty in the JNA, just like any other citizens of that country, in 1972 and 1973?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, you were working at the post office in the Dolac Malta neighbourhood of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While you were working in Sarajevo you lived in an apartment in Dobrinja 3?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since it is important for me in my examination-in-chief that will mostly focus on some characteristics of the terrain where you lived, I am going to show you a map so that you can explain to me or to the Trial Chamber everything that I would like you to explain, and that is the 65 ter number 2872. 65 ter -- oh, all right. Can we zoom in on the map a little bit, please? Can you circle on this map the place where the post office was? Can we see it here or do we need to ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that with the letter P.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Roman alphabet, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now can you mark your place where your house was, your apartment. The apartment in Dobrinja 3.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that with the letter K.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Judges how long you went to work?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to work until the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the 15th of April. Excuse me. Excuse me. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to tell us which year. And just one moment, Mr. Gojkovic. Do not rush. Please wait until the whole question is transcribed and then give a complete answer. So I'm asking you again. How long did you go to work? Can you please give us the date and the year?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to work until the 15th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were hurrying again and you were not paying attention to the transcript. Please do not speak -- do not say anything when I am speaking. I am asking you. These are very big difficulties for all of us who are working here, including the interpreters, so please wait for my complete question to be typed into the transcript and then give it a second or two and then you can begin to answer. Do not start your answer until the cursor on the monitor stops, please. Can you please do that. Why did you go to work until that day, until then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1992, I left work early. I went -- there was the B and H TO, Territorial Defence, on the street already with weapons. When I left the company, I reached Pofalici. Since my family, my children, and -- two children were already in the family house at Stanojevici. Actually, they left the family house in Stanojevici. My wife and I had left work. By the time we got to Pofalici, where I got off the tram in order to go to Grbavica, I was intercepted by three young men in civilian clothing with rifles on their shoulders. They asked for my papers. They took my personal ID card, and they told my wife to continue on. However, after a certain amount of time, near the school of economics you could hear shooting. Then they left. And in the meantime, I continued on my way towards Grbavica. At that point, I crossed the bridge of Bratstvo-Jedinstvo and I crossed into Grbavica and I went to my family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now again, please, I would like you to wait. Can you now mark the place where your family house was on this map.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not here on this map. We would need to move the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask to have the map moved all the way to the right, because I'm going to be dealing with that section of the map. But first we have to save this. I think that if you move the map, the markings will disappear. Is that correct? Can we please save the map in this form first, and then we can continue. Then we can focus on the right-hand side of the map, because my entire examination-in-chief will focus on that section of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're asking to tender this exhibit? It is being tendered into evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D309, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to go all the way to the right. Now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please answer one more question first. We saw this photograph earlier. Did you ever return to work, or did you ever return to your apartment where you lived before you went to your family house?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I never went back to work or to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you please mark the place where your family house was.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you mark the circle with the letter M, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your last name is Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please do not answer anything until I complete my question. Your last name is Gojkovic, and what is the name -- Witness, please do not begin to answer until I finish speaking and until that is transcribed into the transcript. Then you can answer. Your last name is Gojkovic. What is the place where your house, your family house was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the map it says Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please do not start your answer until the cursor stops, because I'm just simply not going to be able to go on. Please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It says Gojkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us when you joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? And we can make it a little bit faster now.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: After I left Sarajevo, I joined the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said you left in April.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But when did you join the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We joined the corps in May when it was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Judges how you acquired weapons?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We got weapons at Tilava, from the civilian protection. Actually, we broke into the warehouses and we took the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you point out the place where this civilian protection was located?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could zoom in a little bit on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Tilava.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If it's not on the map, I know it's a little bit further to the south, but it's no good now moving the map. Can you indicate the direction where it is?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate the direction, roughly, where it was and then put a mark there, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you mark that place with the letter T.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now can you please tell me where the line of separation was -- or first of all, can you answer the question -- this question: Which unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I belonged to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the 2nd Battalion, 2nd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which battalion? What sort of a battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: An infantry battalion. It was a battalion of the infantry unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but what brigade was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Brigade. Did it have a name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Sarajevo 2nd Brigade, Sarajevska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you see this map, can you please tell us where you were? Where were your positions? And can you indicate that with a line on this map in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what is to the left and to the right of that place? What is the geographical area there like?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: To the left were the so-called 8s Osmices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please circle that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you mark that with the letter G.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you put the line on this yellow line. What is this yellow line?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The yellow line is the road Vraca-Trebevic-Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what is this area to the left of this red line? What is that area called?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: To the left of the red line is Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw a line that would mark what you call Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell the Judges -- well, these were the positions where you were at, but tell them when you arrived to take up those positions, that first marking of yours, the red line? So would you put an R by the red line, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the second one where you speak of Zlatiste, put a Z, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the positions that you marked with the R letter, when did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The positions that I marked with an R, were ones we arrived at on the 15th of June -- or between the 15th of June and 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who held those positions up until that time, until that 15th of July and beginning of -- of July -- 15th of June and beginning of July? So who held those lines, the ones you've marked?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Those lines were held by the Territorial Defence of the BH army -- or, rather, BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, on the 15th of June, where did you have to go if you wanted to go to Lukavica or Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: When we wanted to go to Pale and Lukavica, we had to take the macadam road across Krdemic [phoen], Kleka, to Golubici, and Pavlovac and then take the road towards Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you draw that line, at least approximately, the route.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't draw the line because I can't find the places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately. Yes, you can't draw it all exactly on this map, but just draw us an approximate line.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: And the line continues from Tilava to Kleka, to Golubici, Pavlovac and then on towards Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Along the bottom of the map draw a straight line, a straight line, because we can't move the map, in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Draw the full line.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean to the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you're going to Pale, Pale isn't that way. And you mentioned Jahorina, didn't you? Just draw the line to the end -- or never mind. Thank you. Continue towards Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You want me to draw in towards Lukavica or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: An approximate line in the direction of Lukavica, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did the fighting look like until June before you stopped at these positions and along that road?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Before we reached those positions we weren't able to communicate along that route, because they were under fire from Debelo Brdo, and from Ramac to up there. We weren't able to pass by that way. Until this Prvi Sumar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where is this Prvi Sumar? What is this place? Could you draw it in? Well, let's not waste time here. We have to continue.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't draw it in on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, while the witness to trying to find on the map this particular location, could you please clarify what year we're talking. When you said up until June, what year was that. When he talked about the combat activities he said until June, and I wonder what year he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Judge Mindua. I thought the witness had answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever you get a date, Witness, from now until we complete the examination, you have it to give us the date and the year, because without that it's no use. So what June are you talking about? The June of what year, when you took up these positions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the position you marked with R, what did the positions look like there? What were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The positions at the letter R, were the positions when you go from the left-hand side of the road along the road. They were along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not enough. It's not enough to say along the road, left-hand side of the road. What were they like? What was there at your positions? What did you have there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The R position from Andja's house towards the Dragaseve house and Jevtovica house, there were Muslim forces in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, would you please concentrate. Were you in houses or in something else? Where were you when you were up at that position? Where were you in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We were along the edge of the road right up by the woods, and then later on we dug trenches to protect ourselves from the actions going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did those trenches look like? How long were they, where you were? What was the length of the trenches?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The trenches were at every 20 or 30 metres, one next to the other, following on from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how far were the trenches of the BH army from where you were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The BH army soldiers were at a distance of 20 to 30 metres, by Andja's house, and a little further towards the other houses, about 50 metres there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on this map can you mark Andja's house and Jevtovic's house? And put an A for Andja's houses?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the Jevtovic's houses, you can put a J there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was round about, all around you? And we're talking about the positions of the BH army and the positions of the Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a thick forest where the positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the combat operations looked like throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not clear to me if we're still talking about 1992. If we are, I submit that this evidence is irrelevant. A bit of background about the witness, when did you join the army, and what did you first do when you joined the army, is fine, and it helps understand the evidence that is relevant, but this level of detail about events greatly preceding the indictment period is, I submit, irrelevant. And even if this is -- the testimony is that this continued into 1994 or 1995, I am still hard-pressed to understand the relevance to a case that alleges attacks on civilians to this level of detail of the opposing armies, the military operations here. So I submit that this evidence is irrelevant, and that's my objection, and that's my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, you've heard the objection raised by Mr. Docherty, and this brings us back to what I was saying yesterday. It is something that we seem to be debating on a daily basis, the relevance of some of the evidence. I'm looking at the clock, and if I'm not mistaken, you've been talking for an hour and your speaking time for this examination-in-chief is of an hour and a half. So you've devoted a full hour to the presentation of the background of this witness, talking about his situation in the army in 1992. Now, I believe that the time has come to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, would you check the time with the relevant official. I have not used up one hour. There's no question of that. But you can see the problems that I have encountered in examining this witness. And if we were to see how far I've come thus far, then the comments would have been in order, but I have to deal with matters of this kind as a lead-up to questions that are relevant for the entire period of the conflict. But I have not used up one hour so far, far from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. You are right. According to the registrar, you haven't used that full hour, but please keep to the essential questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now, all this time, from 1992 to 1995, were you at this same place, at the position that you're talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In -- from 1992 to 1995, we were at those same positions until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that this position -- that you took up this position in June 1992, only then, and then you talked about the problems of communication and linked to those roads. Now, tell me, what happened most frequently, first of all at these positions, the positions that you were at in that forest, as you said, facing the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived to take up those positions it was our assignment to hold the communication lines, to maintain control of the communication lines, but we encountered constant provocation from the BH army side; mostly, when the buses arrived carrying civilians going to Pale, or the elderly and sick who were passing by that road going to Pale, to the hospital there that was at Koreni.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean at the position at Andja's houses, Andja's houses. That's very close to the road, Andja's houses, and as soon as they heard the sound of a car or bus, whoever was passing by, they would start shooting, firing at the road straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any victims, any casualties?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: While I was up at that position there was Andja Pandurevic. She was killed in the bus from a shot fired from the BH army side. And there was another case later on, someone from UNPROFOR. An UNPROFOR vehicle was moving from Pale towards Lukavica, and it was taking some humanitarian aid but was hit. The cabin was hit, and the driver swerved off the road. And Colovic, I don't know his first name, but he ran over a man called Colovic who was 61 years old and on his way towards Pale on foot. So the driver, the UNPROFOR vehicle, having swerved off the road crashed into this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. You've already said that, but can you please tell me how this firing went with you on one side and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the other side some 30 metres apart? What did this look like, this action relating to this road?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't fire at all unless provoked by them. Unless they fired at our positions or on the road, we refrained very much in order to avoid anything major. In some cases, we had to retaliate, return fire, in order for the civilians in the buses and passenger cars to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you go along this road that was under your control, you say that the road runs to Zlatiste. Please do not answer yet. It continues towards Zlatiste. And this road at Zlatiste, what was the ability to actually be able to observe from that place beneath the road? Was it possible to actually look at the area beneath the road or below the road at that spot?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: From Zlatiste to Osmice it's about 800 metres, but you could not observe for some hundred metres below the road because from Bosut, from Debelo Brdo, and from Zelengorska Street where there is a forest, there was firing at those sectors, and from Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark with arrows which directions was it fired at. You mentioned Debelo Brdo, Zelengorska Street and Colina Kapa. Please wait, wait for the typing to stop and then you can mark first by arrows the way you describe that from the direction of Debelo Brdo. So first can you make an arrow from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that arrow with the letter "CH". The one from the direction of Debelo Brdo can you mark that with the letter D. The one in the middle with the letter -- and that is from the direction of this road.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please do not speak until I am finished. And can you mark that with the letter G.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This road, this part of the road, what was happening with that throughout the conflict, from 1992 until 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The road from Zlatiste is where the B and H forces fired at our positions and the road itself, and we were forced to use sandbags and to make a protective shield of some two and a half metres height so that the road could be used more safely for travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, I forgot to ask you in the beginning, when you took the weapons from the Territorial Defence, the civilian protection, at that time when the -- when we're talking about early 1992, May, in that area, in those areas where you were at the time when you took the rifle into your hands, were there any more serious, heavier weapons there as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have anything. We had semi-automatic and automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please follow me. My time is very limited. I didn't ask you -- all right. When you set off, what did you have of the weapons in that place where you were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We had semi-automatic and automatic rifles where we were. We didn't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But now I would like to ask you, in 1992, did you notice up there from Tilava, Lukavica, you mentioned Gojkovici, your own place where you come from, did you notice anywhere there any more serious things such as heavy weapons? That's what I'm thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: When we took the weapons from Tilava there were no heavy weapons in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And were there such weapons anywhere else, if not in Tilava? Under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was some in the place of Kozarevici. That's where the mortars were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was this? Can you please indicate that? Approximately, if it's not ... I didn't see you marking anything. I still haven't seen what you marked. Can you make a larger circle so that we can see where it is?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you mark that with the letter F?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me here at Zlatiste, where you have already marked all of these other things, were there any soldiers there at positions, and where were they and what sort of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: At Zlatiste where our positions were, we had automatic rifles and semi-automatic rifles. These are just infantry weapons that we had in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you just had rifles and infantry weapons, but what were the people who held those rifles in? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There were trenches at the positions which we set up because of the fire from enemy formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was any heavy weaponry there at all at any time during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no heavy weapons there at all throughout the war in that area there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And throughout the conflict, especially during the time from August 1994 until November 1995, beside the firing at that section of the road, were there any serious attacks in that period in view of the importance of that road?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was an attack in 1994, sometime in September. It was a minor attack that we thwarted very quickly. I don't remember the exact date, but in 1995, I recall an attack on the 15th of June, where in the area of Andjina Kuca and Jevtovica Kuca formations of the B and H managed to pass at 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning past that line, kill four of our soldiers: Milisav Topacovic; Zarko Djukic; Dzebo, I don't know his first name; and Mile Milidrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us if you remember when General Dragomir Milosevic assumed the post of commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: General Dragomir Milosevic assumed this post in early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1994?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was in early 1994 that he assumed that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what happened in 1994? Do you know anything about, for example, what happened to the mortars that were, as you explained earlier, as you said, which were at the letter F? Do you know if anything in those terms was decided on in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, heavy weaponry was pulled out from the area of Kozarevici, and these weapons were taken. I cannot really tell you the exact location, but it was in the direction of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And during 1994, at some point did you leave these positions where you were at Andjina Kuca and Jevtovina Kuca, and if you went to another location where they were clashes between the two warring sides?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We went to Trnovo where the offensive was underway from 1995, by the army of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So we would go there in shifts of 15 days each.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about 1994, and you're speaking about 1995. I'm asking you again about 1994.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We went in 1994 to Trnovo as well to help Trnovo up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And let's cut things short. Can you please tell us what the situation was like at positions in 1994 and on? Let's say from early 1994 until sometime. Were there any quiet periods where you were, or was it different there than it was in other places?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was different in that area because that road was very important to us. There were constant attacks, provocations. We didn't retaliate that much because this was very important for us, this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when was it the most difficult? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the most difficult in 1994, sometime in November, and also in 1995, on the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after the 15th of May onwards, and why do you mention this particular date, the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, the offensive began, the BH offensive, throughout that area, the area held by the fighters of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't give us the year. You said the 15th of May, but you didn't give us the year. And secondly, are you certain that it was the 15th of May when all this began? So you have to give us the date and the year every time. The date plus the year.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 15th of May, 1995, when this breakthrough was made between Andja's house. And this was one of the worst attacks, when the Muslim forces -- the BH forces crossed the road, toppled the trees along the road and entered a territory that we controlled. They went into that territory for about a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, 20 minutes ago or so when you were talking about this, you said that that was the offensive and that that offensive took place on the 15th of June, 1992. Now you say 1995. You said the 15th of May. So which is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I meant the 15th of June. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know whether at the position you were at and when the offensive started, were there any casualties among the soldiers on your side and the civilians, any fatalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of June, 1995, Milisav Topacovic was killed, as I already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat what you've already said. What I'm asking you now is this: You say it began on the 15th of June, and as the events unfolded, did what I asked you about happen? Did you see anything? Did you learn anything?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I was at home on the 15th in the morning, 15th of June, when we were called to go and defend that territory, the BH army shelled the area of Stanojevici, Kozarevici, so that no reinforcements could reach the area. And one shell, an 82-millimetre shell fell between Sreto Gojkovic's house and shed, but luckily no one was killed. And then there was extra shelling following that one because of the reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did the offensive last? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The offensive lasted into the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't asking you about that particular day. I was asking you in general. Did the offensive begin on the 15th of June and ended on the same day or not? I'm asking you how many days the offensive lasted.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the area -- while I was in the area, it lasted throughout that day and the next day too. They kept attacking. The BH forces kept attacking those positions, the positions we managed to hold, and then on the 15th of June, 1995, towards the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, you've already explained to us some things, and I won't go back to those. You said that, and you've repeated that several times, that the fighting never stopped because of the importance of that road. Now, I'm asking you to the best of your knowledge and linked to that offensive that started on the 15th of June, how long it lasted. I assume you had information about how long it lasted in all the areas where there was combat activity going on. And not in one day, I mean generally. Well, if it only lasted one day, then say it lasted one day and I'll be satisfied with that. But if it went on for several days, tell us please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The offensive against our positions lasted for three days. Now, the other positions, as far as information reached me, the offensive lasted for two or three days there, too, against those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me then, please, did you ever see Dragomir Milosevic, General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw General Dragomir Milosevic two or three times a month. The general would come by. He would come up to the positions and he was always ready to come and see us in the trenches and to boost our morale and to tell us to keep control of the road, of that communication line, because it was necessary. And quite simply, he came by to congratulate us for holding the line and for the fact that there was no problem along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, did he stay there for any length of time or was he just passing by because he had to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The general would stop by to see us in the trenches. He would talk to us every time he was going that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know where he was on his way to, where he was going?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The general was moving in the direction of Pale, Trnovo, Vogosca, Ilijas, Ilidza. That way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I think we now need to take the break. It is 12.25. You have taken one hour and 10 minutes, and so you still have 20 minutes left. So when we resume, you will have the floor for 20 minutes at most. And so let me give you the rest of the programme for the day. We now have a break for one hour beginning now, so we shall resume at 1.35. And when we resume, we will continue until 3.05. Then there will be a 20-minute break, after which we will again resume at 3.25 until 5.00. The hearing is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed, and we give the floor to the Defence. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll be very brief. I don't think I will even use up my 20 minutes that I'm entitled to. I would like to keep this map, so I kindly ask you to provide the witness another pen of another colour, because I'm going to ask the witness to mark a few more things on the map, but I would like to keep the image as it is at the moment. Can we have another colour, not the red?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you take this new pen, and can you mark the street which you referred as Zelengorska.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What you have just marked at Zlatiste on the road as the positions of the VRS army, with respect to the street that you have just marked, Zelengorska, where were the positions of the 1st Corps of the BH army? Could you please draw another blue line on this map.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does it go anywhere further in depth or tell me, I don't want to spend any more time on this map, what was the distance between these positions in this place, between the positions of the two militaries? What was the distance in metres, for example?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The distance in metres was about a hundred metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where you were in the forest?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the forest, about 20 to 30 metres from Andja's house or 50 metres up by Sovici house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question has to do with this: You've already explained that in the positions where you were, the intensity of fire was continuous throughout all that time. You have also provided another explanation about the arms. Can you tell us how did the conflicts between the two militaries evolve when it came to the weapons, in the position where you were some 20 to 50 metres away from them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The conflict at the distance of 50 metres was with infantry weapons. Fire was opened at us, and we would return fire from the same infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness. I would kindly ask for this map to be kept in this form as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I believe you should ask the witness to identify the two blue lines on the street -- on the map. One was the Zelengorska Street, and one was the front line, the ABiH front line, but it's important that we keep track of which is which.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. In haste, I had failed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The line that represents Zelengorska Street, can you put a letter M next to it -- actually, letter D. And can you also mark the positions of the BiH army with a letter -- I can't think of a letter. I don't want to repeat the letters that we used before. Put an F -- no, you've already used F, put an E.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we shall admit that exhibit as evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D310, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The trial attorney would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: My name is John Docherty. I'm one of the prosecuting attorneys on this case. I have some questions for you this afternoon concerning the things you've been talking about while being questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic. If I ask a question that's not clear to you, would you please ask me to clear it up rather than just guessing at what the answer; is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You testified that you were in the -- that you joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in 1992. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but I believe that I remember that it was in 1992. Yes, it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Once you were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you stay in it until the end of the armed conflict, or did you leave before late 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I spent the entire war in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I did not leave until 1995, when peace accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And was it your testimony that you spent the entire war in this area on the map monitor in front of you, it's the area in -- I'll call it the upper right that's got a lot of markings in it. That's where you spent your war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I spent the entire war there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You also testified that in the areas where you were, there were no heavy weapons. Do you remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that where I had been, where our positions had been, there was no heavy weaponry, not in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But you also testified that there were mortars at the position marked on this map as F; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You, yourself, were never stationed at the position marked with an F, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never stationed there, nor do I know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So when you said that there were mortars at the position marked with the F, that was something you had heard from somebody else or something you had read. It wasn't something that you yourself had observed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That was very close, below the place where I resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we've misunderstood each other. You testified that you were not stationed at the position marked F, and so I then asked you, then when you testified about there being mortars at that position, that was something you heard about from someone else. Can you tell us, sir, am I right or wrong that you heard about the mortars from other people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that from those people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What rank did you have in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Were you an officer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not. I was not an officer, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So when you heard about the mortars, that was not through any sort of official reporting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard from the people who were close to the mortars that there were mortars, because they were in the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I understand, and what I'm trying to get at now is, when you were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, were you a private soldier?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a private soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you did not have access to the sort of reports that would be circulated to officers who might need to know about things like weapon placement outside their positions of responsibility. You were not -- you did not have access to that flow, that type of information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have access to that type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So really your testimony is about -- your firsthand knowledge is about the area where you were stationed throughout the war. Those are the things that you would have seen yourself or heard for yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I heard and what I saw is true, and I am here to speak the truth. I can't speak of the things that I only heard about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No. And just to be clear, I wasn't making any accusations, but I was just saying that the things you can testify about, that you saw yourself, are the things that happened in your trench on that road between 1992 and 1995. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gojkovic, I don't know if you're aware of this, but do you -- do you know or have you heard that before a witness gives testimony at this Tribunal, some basic information about what the witness will say is communicated to the other side's lawyers? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say you were or you were not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, the document that describes your testimony, a so-called 65 ter summary, says that you were a member of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. Your testimony today has been you were a member of the 2nd Brigade. Is 2nd Brigade correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I misspoke. It was the 1st Sarajevo Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you were in the 1st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you as a member of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, this area where you were stationed is a part of that unit's area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that is along the road, I believe your testimony was, Vraca-Lukavica-Pale. Is that the road that you were alongside during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You testified that you observed firing on buses, cars, other vehicles along at that road during the time that you were there. Do you remember giving that testimony, Mr. Gojkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is it not true, however, that your -- you and your colleagues were also dug in along that road?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that they were there along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you were soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In uniform and carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We carried arms, and we wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is it not also true that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had sniper positions along that road throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: From Zlatiste up there to Andja's house there were no sharpshooters. In my platoon there were no sharpshooters either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And how long a distance is it from Zlatiste to this house in metres? How long -- how large a position of the front line are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How far is it in metres along that road from Zlatiste to Andja's house?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 300 metres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so that 300 metres would be the distance that you, yourself, are speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Again what distance did you mention? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sure. If you started at Zlatiste and you walked -- or you went along the road until you got to Andja's house, I understand your testimony to be that would be about 300 metres. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you take the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that is the area that your platoon was responsible for. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, you are not. The platoon was from Andja's house to Gasa Jevtovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And your testimony is in the area from Zlatiste to Andja's house, there were no sharpshooters. Did I understand you properly? No SRK sharpshooters.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever we went there, there were never any sharpshooters, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, we've talked at the beginning of this cross-examination about the things that you could see personally and the things that you could not. And do you accept that in other areas of that road, areas that you could not see yourself, the SRK did have sharpshooters?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't speak about things that I didn't see, can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could please see 65 ter number 03390.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what I'm going to be showing you, Mr. Gojkovic, is a photograph. Just take a moment and look at that. This is from a publication, and it is described as a Bosnian Serb army position on Mount Trebevic. Now, the road you were alongside went Vraca-Pale -- Vraca, Trebevic, Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you were a soldier for quite a number of years, 1992 through and including 1995. Does what you see in this photograph in front of you look like a military target, if you were an opposing soldier?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this place. I don't know where this is. Again, I didn't understand what you want me to tell you. What do you mean by military target?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, thank you for asking. I'll try and clear it up because I do want us to communicate clearly. You began -- we began this discussion by talking about your testimony concerning firing on buses and private vehicles along that road. And I believe that so far you've testified that you and your colleagues, who were armed soldiers, were dug in alongside that road. And we're now talking about the presence of other military targets along that road, and that's why we got onto the topic of sharpshooter positions. You indicated that between Zlatiste and Andja's house there were no sharpshooters, and then we talked about whether there might have been sharpshooters in places that you did not personally see, and that's where this photograph came from because this photograph is of a position on Mount Trebevic. And if I understand correctly, the road that you and your fellow soldiers were stationed alongside ran to Mount Trebevic; that was part of its route. So that's my first question. Did that road go to Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then my second question would be what we see in this photograph. There's a soldier in uniform; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a soldier in reserve. A soldier, but a soldier in reserve. An elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Wearing a uniform; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Some didn't have anything to wear, those who fled Sarajevo, and they put the uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And to this person's right there is a rifle, is there not? You see it lying there? The stock is towards the camera.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the man has got binoculars as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so this is a photograph of a military position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to switch topics now. I'm going to talk to you for a few minutes about where the weapons and ammunition came from that you and your colleagues were using. You indicated that you had obtained weapons from a warehouse. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that we took the weapons from Tilava, from the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. And you indicated that those were semi-automatic and automatic infantry weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did they look like the rifle in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: They were smaller rifles, semi-automatic and automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm finished with this photograph, so could we tender it at this time, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At that becomes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no objection to this photograph being tendered as an exhibit, but I must say that it was not explained to the witness if he knows anything about a position like this, whether he's personally ever seen a position like this anywhere. Other questions I'm going to put in the re-examination, but the witness didn't say anything about where this position could be in view of the fact that he was in the woods. But I have no objections to this photograph being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If Mr. Tapuskovic has no objection, I'm not sure it's incumbent on me to respond, but I do believe that the witness testified several times that there were no sharpshooters that he had ever seen personally, and since that is photograph of someone with binoculars and a rifle, I -- I took it that the witness had not seen anything like this. However, I'll ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you were never positioned on Mount Trebevic, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I know, I don't think that this is a Trebevic position. Not that part that I know at least. This photograph is unclear to me where this is. You do need to know the locations to be able to tell where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Gojkovic, the question was, you were not positioned on Mount Trebevic, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If this is Trebevic, this place, I wasn't there then, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second objection, Your Honours, since snipers are being insisted on here all the time. This weapon that you see here, is that a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect, I think that's a matter for re-examination, not an objection to the admission of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, the Trial Chamber has already admitted this exhibit, and therefore during -- well, during the cross-examination, the witness simply answered the questions addressed to him by the trial attorney. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as Exhibit P818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, during the war where did you and your fellow soldiers obtain the ammunition they needed for the weapons that they were using to fight the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This was all done legally through the company, the battalion, and I don't know what the procedure was after that, where the company senior officer obtained them from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 02305A, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We could indeed, but I think I would like to hear the witness's answer to the question put to him by Mr. Tapuskovic before we leave this photo. Mr. Witness, the weapon that you see on the photo here, what sort of weapon is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a machine-gun. I don't know what type it is, what M number, but it's not a sniper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this give rise to any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you say it's a not a sniper. You, yourself, never had sniper duty during the war, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You, yourself, were never trained as a sniper, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You are not familiar with the types of weapons that snipers can use in different situations, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never, and I didn't want to learn about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I am going to assume, but please correct me if I am wrong, that you have not read the expert report submitted by the Prosecution in this case by a Dutch army officer about the sniping incidents at issue in this case. Am I right that you did not read that report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, therefore, would not know that that expert identified a machine-gun as the most likely weapon to have been used in several of the incidents that are before this court. And I don't have the report in front of me so I can't tell you how many, but you are not aware of that, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, the assessment in the expert report is something that the Chamber has to make up its mind on when it makes a ruling on that, because this is something that can only be subjected to the opinion or the judgement of the Chamber. It cannot be up to the witness to discuss what the expert is talking about in his report. This is something that is a matter for the Trial Chamber. If the witness were to be asked to deal with the findings of an expert, then we would really go quite far in all respects at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think, Mr. Tapuskovic is -- is right. It's not up to the witness to read the expert reports that are submitted to the Trial Chamber. At any rate, the witness has said that he has never been a sniper, never learned how to be a sniper, and does not know how to distinguish weapons used by snipers. We have the picture before us, and therefore we can assess the situation. I think it's quite enough, and we can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I, of course, will move on to something else in line with your ruling. I do want to briefly correct what I believe is a misapprehension. I was not asking the witness and would never ask a witness to discuss an expert report. I simply asked the witness if he was aware of the contents of the expert report. But with that I will move on. And again if we could see 65 ter 02305a.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gojko, we're going to be talking about two pages from a larger document. The first page is coming up on the monitor in front of you, and this relates to the issue that we were just starting to talk about, which is where the ammunition that you and your fellow soldiers used came from. In front of you, do you see a document? It's in your language on the right-hand side. And does this document indicate that it is a transcript of a tape recording of the 50th session of the National Assembly held on the 15th and 16th of April, 1995, in Sanski Mostar? Have I read that accurately?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to move now to the second page, and as I say it's the second page of this -- of this extract. It's from a larger document, and this is a portion of a speech, transcribed speech, by General Ratko Mladic. And as soon as the English comes up, I'll just have a few questions for you concerning it. Do you see the paragraph, it's the first -- excuse me, the second full paragraph on the page, and it begins: "As an illustration, I will compare data of the consumption..." Do you see the paragraph that begins with those words?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph begins: "As an illustration, I will compare data of the consumption of certain types of materiel according to source from the beginning of the war up until 31 December 1994, with the needs for 1995 and the current situation." Now, Mr. Gojkovic, are you aware that in late 1994, I believe in August, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia placed sanctions on transfer of arms to the Bosnian Serb army in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Are you aware of that event?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't understand this question at all. I was just a regular soldier. I don't know how much was spent, when, where. Please believe me, this is really not a question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you accept that General Ratko Mladic would know what he was talking about when he describes to the RS Assembly where the ammunition for its army is coming from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question? I just was not paying attention to -- I was looking at the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I try to be more interesting and keep you focused, but -- my question really was about the authority or the credibility of the speaker here. This is a speech by General Ratko Mladic, and I was asking if you would accept that General Mladic is someone who, if he's speaking to the RS Assembly, is going to know where the ammunition for the army he commands is coming from. That is a subject he would know about. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Please believe me that I'm not the right person to be able to answer that. I have no answer to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you would not know whether Ratko Mladic would know where his army's ammunition came from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot say anything that I'm not able to check 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's try this: Do you see that this paragraph, the one I've directed your attention to, talks about the army's consumption of different kinds of ammunition, and also talks about what sources that ammunition was obtained from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're asking me -- well, you should be asking me about the positions and where my position was. This is something that I don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that's why I'm not asking you about it. I'm simply asking you if the document says that this is where -- this is the different types of ammunition, and this is where it came from. I respect your answer that you personally don't know about these things, and that's why I'm carefully asking you just about what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you, because I'm not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I think we should too. Mr. President, I will, however, tender this -- this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I believe it fails the relationship test. I'm not in favour of it, but let me consult with Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, you've decided not to ask for the floor? Very well. Mr. Docherty -- Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, actually, I simply don't know what to say, I agree with the view of Judge Harhoff on this. The witness don't know anything about this. But I would almost agree for this document to be tendered so that I could provide my own point of view, but I do believe that it cannot be admitted according to this criteria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. You may seek to tender this document through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. I quite agree that if it was dependent upon the witness being able to authenticate the document, I would not have offered it. However, before getting into the area the witness did not know about, we looked at the first page which indicated that this was a transcript of a speech given by a particular person to a particular Assembly on a particular date. So I do not -- I do not rest my submission for admission upon the witness. I guess I take the view that the document has authenticated itself by the presence of page 1. That's why I offer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If there are other parts of this document to which the witness can testify and knows about, then you can tender it, but you can't tender it into evidence on the basis of what we've heard so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Very good, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So please pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gojkovic, just to sum up, you understand in general terms what this case is about; is that correct? You have some understanding of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you understand that the evidence you have given today has been limited to this small area on the map between Zlatiste and Andja's house, if that is correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zlatiste, Andja's houses, Dragaseve. Those houses, yes. That is the area to which my testimony is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. I will ask the document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're requesting this, for this document, that it be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm requesting that these two pages be marked for identification, because there may be later a witness through whom it can be offered. But it's not being offered, just MFI at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be marked for identification as P819.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have any additional questions for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Questions. One has to do with this photograph. Can we please show the witness this document, P818.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've already said this, and you gave explanations about the weapons. Judge Harhoff asked you about that and other things that have to do with this photograph. Based on this photograph can you say at all where this actual location is?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said before that I don't know where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is the first question relating to this photograph. The second question is the way this man is looking through the binoculars or using them from that place. Can you see anything there that would help you to recognise any particular area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't recognise anything from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you see any part of Sarajevo from this particular place, any place? I don't want to specify anything, any of the suburbs, the centre, the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If it was from Trebevic, then you would have to see a part of town, but from here you cannot see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would have just one more question for you to clarify. You described the positions at Zlatiste up to Andjina Kuca, and Andja's houses. You were never at those positions by the side of the road the way you described it, next to Andja's houses, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You described your positions as being between Andja's and Jevtovic's houses. You mentioned that before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the positions below Andjina's houses, you never took up positions there, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never took up positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic. The Judges do not have any further questions either. Witness, the Trial Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague to add your contribution to this trial, and so all I have left to do is to wish you a smooth return home and great success in all of your future endeavours, and you may now leave the Court room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, before calling the next witness, I'd like to quickly solve one procedural problem that was raised by the Defence. It has to do with your public motion for leave to amend the list of witnesses and to file an expert report after the deadline set by the Trial Chamber with confidential Annex A. You say that it's a public motion, so I will give you the floor very briefly to explain to us exactly what this motion is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague Isailovic will be doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Indeed, the Defence yesterday, on the 12th of July, filed a motion to obtain leave to amend the list of witnesses and also to file an expert report after the deadline set by the Trial Chamber. That was set for the 13th of July, that is to say today. And the problem that the Defence has had is that the expert, the forensic expert, T-29 on our 65 ter bis -- I'm sorry, 65 ter list, this forensic expert has invoked personal reasons for not appearing before this Chamber, personal reasons why he cannot appear, and the Defence therefore had to find someone else who would be able to offer some assistance to the Defence as a forensic expert. And so the procedure for appointing this expert by the relevant service or department, that is to say the Registry, it's a procedure that took approximately one month, between the 12th of June and the 12th -- well, the 11th of July, to be precise. That is the date upon which the Defence was informed that Dr. Ivica Milosavljevi [phoen] was appointed, who could therefore serve as the expert in question. So if the Trial Chamber agrees to this appointment -- would the Chamber agree to the -- to his being added to our list of witnesses. And, of course, this would also prolong things a bit. The Defence has already contacted this expert who was officially appointed and, therefore, has already begun his work, but it -- it will be a fairly concise, succinct report, expert report, meant to help the Defence in raising a few issues falling within the realm of his expertise.
