And we could quite quickly obtain this report and file it, but first of all, we need to know whether his name can be added to the list of the witnesses before we can actually file his report. So we received the answer of the Prosecution, the Prosecution's reply. They have no objection in principle to his replacing Dr. Slobodan Kovacevic, who had been foreseen as our forensic expert, the forensic expert of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Isailovic. Does the Prosecutor have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We don't have an objection to swapping the experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Waespi. Very well. Indeed -- indeed, yesterday the Defence filed a motion to amend its list of witnesses and replace the expert witness who had been foreseen to date by another expert witness. The Defence also requests or asks the Trial Chamber to change the deadline for filing the expert's conclusion, to extend it to the 20th of July, 20th of July, 2007. The Prosecution, according to what the Defence has told us, notified by e-mail the Defence and the Trial Chamber that it does not object, and Mr. Waespi has just confirmed that the Prosecution does not object. However, the Prosecutor did not say anything with regard to extending the deadline for filing the conclusions. I see that Mr. Waespi may have something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We understand the situation Defence is in, and 20th of July is no problem for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Prosecution does not object to an extension of the deadline set. The Trial Chamber has just deliberated and grants the motion of the Defence. The Defence may therefore amend its list of witnesses and is authorised to file the expert's conclusions no later than the 20th of July, which means that the deadline is the 20th of July. It is thus decided. We shall now call the next witness. Mr. Tapuskovic, which witness shall it be? We're in closed session, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. [Private session].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours -- sorry for the interruption. Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tapuskovic, we are in open session. Please keep that in mind. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like DD003980, the document there, to be shown to the witness for identification. He's a protected witness, so may he have a look at the document? And then I'd like to tender it under seal on the part of the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D311 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. Thank you very much. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, but in order to present the witness's CV, I'd like us to move back into private session, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness T-15, can you tell us the reason for which you moved to take up residence in your parents' house in the place you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Some time at the beginning of 1992, or more exactly in February and March of that same year, the opportunity arose -- or, rather, the circumstances and situation was such that for the people in Sarajevo -- the people in Sarajevo began to be afraid. There were various things going on, and this was reflected in the following manner: They noticed some unknown people in the area where they would move around every day and had been doing so for many years. Suddenly some new people arrive, and these people carried weapons, and they stopped vehicles and passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you were a policeman, weren't you, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was stopped, too, even as a policeman. People would ask for my ID. These were people in civilian clothing. They stopped even me. And they had infantry weapons, a small arms, a pistol or a rifle, perhaps. And all this instilled fear in the population. Not only me but in the locals, the residents, and the people couldn't understand this behaviour, this conduct. And one of the more drastic cases of this kind occurred in April 1992. I was driving my brother, who was ill, and I was driving my own car, when I was stopped in front of the hospital at Hrastovi. That's what it was called. It was a pulmonary disease hospital for chest disorders. And I was stopped by a group of armed individuals whom I did not know. They asked me where I was going. They made me get out of the car. They took me into the hospital. They left my sick brother. They separated us, so my brother stayed behind. They started beating me. I don't remember how long this went on for. They told me that they had killed my brother, in fact, and that I would end up the same way as him. To the best of my recollections, I subsequently established that I had been there for maybe some 40 minutes, up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, you were wearing a police uniform, weren't you, at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was wearing a uniform, but they seized my pistol and my ID, police ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of April -- you mentioned the 4th of April, but in the coming days, did anything else happen that frightened you even more?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after this -- well, I'll call it arrest. Perhaps you would call it differently, but I'm going to call it my arrest. They released me upon the insistence of somebody. I don't know who insisted that I be released, but they saw I suppose that I was a policeman although they didn't give me back my police ID or my pistol, regular issue pistol. And I didn't go back to Sarajevo any more. But on the 6th of April, the village I was born in was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm not going to interrupt you. You can carry on, but please don't mention the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon of that 6th of April, that place was attacked with a large number of people, and that instilled even greater fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just stop there for a moment. I told you not to mention the name of the place, but tell me where the place is located in relation to one of the recognisable geographical points or parts of Sarajevo, if you can put it in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If you look from the centre of Sarajevo, it would be towards the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the dominant hill called there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the direction of, let's say, Krs hill. We called it Krs hill and Grdonj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, please carry on and tell us what you were saying about the attack on that village?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the attack a man was killed. The people defended themselves as best they could with the means they had. We didn't know what the reason for that was, for what had happened was. The media, in the evening, broadcast the news that an incident had taken place and that no reason was known for the incident, which triggered the incident. There were some -- said to be some people there who had come in from outside, but I say with full responsibility that they were locals. After that 6th of April, all communications ceased between the part of Sarajevo where I lived and the part I went back to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say communications were interrupted, can you explain to us what that means in relation to your village? You mentioned Grdonj, Krs. So could you explain to us more specifically what that meant or what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The road from that place to -- into town -- well, there was just one road leading from there into town, and you couldn't move along that road any more. The people were stranded in that place without any possibility of going into town by car. And you couldn't go on foot because of these armed people standing guard at certain elevations and features that you had to pass through where there were some foot paths and so on. So as of that day, the people could no longer pass along that way and go in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, I'd like to go on to another area because we don't have much time, and I'd like to start off by showing you two photographs. They are exhibits, Prosecution exhibits. So may we look at D256, first, please. Let's just take a brief look at it. No, I've made a mistake. I beg your pardon. I wanted P361 to be displayed, please, would no markings on it. We'll come back to this photograph, but I made a mistake. I wanted Prosecution document P361 to be shown, but I mixed the photographs up in haste. So P361, please. And can you just give me brief answers. What is this? What are we looking at here above the houses?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is Grdonj hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may we have a look at another Prosecution Exhibit, P748. What is this? What's the elevation above those houses there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This elevation is a place called Krs. That's what we called it, Krs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now my next question. What we can see on this photograph, is that directly linked to the previous photograph? Is the previous photograph just a continuation of this one?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know if they were taken from the same position, from the same point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to make a request. These two Prosecution photographs I have joined together, and I'd like these two joined photographs to be shown to the witness so that he can confirm that in fact those two parts make one whole. So we can display it on the ELMO perhaps, and then the witness can tell us whether those two parts of the photograph, in fact, are one whole and then to link up some positions that I'm going to ask him about and show them on this photograph. I did this myself with the witness's assistance, and I think it might be useful to the Trial Chamber to get a better picture of this area, because these photographs show you the whole area when they're joined together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So show the photos to the witness. Perhaps it would be good to also put them on the ELMO so we can all see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tapuskovic, were the two photos taken from the same point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suppose that they were taken from below the cables about the same time as it is indicated, but the most important thing is this: They depict the configuration of the hill, and that's what they are good for. In that respect, we should not have any problem. I can examine the witness separately, but I believe it would be useful for you to see two -- the two together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry and I understand my learned friend was responding to a question from His Honour Judge Harhoff, but I think one should be careful when suggesting this these two photographs represent a certain fact which actually should come from the witness. So in my submission, it was -- it can be possibly leading to make the suggestion that these two photographs show a certain configuration when really it's up to the witness to make that determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, do you recall if we took a picture that could represent the entire feature here when we were at the site visit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I do not. However, I can look into the issue and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because even on the two photos that have been glued together now, I'm uncertain about whether there is any distance between -- whether there is any geographical distance between the two photos. It seems to me that the ridge is broken where the two photos are put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to examine the witness showing him the photos separately. I didn't do it too well. Maybe this photograph should have been lifted by about half a centimetre and then they would tally perfectly. Because the wall that was there -- this is where the photos were taken, between these two geographical regions. If this photo was a bit higher, then it would be perfect. I understand the Prosecutor's objection. I'm going to do my best to separate the photos and ask the witness for some explanation. As things are now it would take less time, but if the Trial Chamber thinks that this is an amateur work or that the photos have been tampered with, I will have no choice but agree with that and I will then separate the photos and examine the witness using the two photos separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, go ahead, yes, rather then the basis of the separate pictures so to avoid all confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we now first see P478, the first photo, without anything, which is 65 ter 3165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I would prefer that we now take the break while you put some order in your pictures, and we will resume again in 20 minutes. And when we do resume in 20 minutes, we will have altogether an hour and a half still, and I would like you to bring to an end -- come to an end quite quickly so that the Prosecutor can then question the witness so that he can leave this evening. So the hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I'm asking for the witness to stay outside because I have a small announcement to make. It is half past 3.00. We have an hour and a half left until 5.00, and I would very much like to be able to release this witness at 5.00 p.m., because we don't want to keep him in The Hague until Monday. Now, it might be a problem for him, and I am sure that the registrar is not going to be happy about this because of the financial implications. So we're better off releasing today than Monday in the evening. Those reasons, I am urging the Defence, who has already -- who has another 20 minutes left -- or has used 20 minutes, sorry, and so they have another 30, that will be 50 in total. The Prosecutor has got 50 minutes in total and 10 minutes for possible additional questions from the Defence. So Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm sorry, we are running out of time. What is it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is absolutely impossible with this witness. First of all, I have received a lot of photographs from the Prosecution after he took the solemn declaration. This will require a lot of time. The pictures that the Court has taken will be very are useful, but I'm sure that there will be a lot of re-examination on my part. This is a very important witness and I really can't promise the Trial Chamber that I can complete my job in such a short period of time, in the period that I have been given, the hour that was granted to me a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, the reduction of time is only 10 minutes. You were given 10 minutes. In total you will be given 50; you have used 20, so you're left with 30 minutes. So the reduction in time is only 10 minutes. So that's our decision. Please, we go to private session and Mr. Registrar please do introduce the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we may, can we please keep this photo that the Court took when they went on the site visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this regard, Witness, could you please look at the photo and the truth is I've not asked you anything about what I want to ask you about, but I'm not sure I will be in the position to ask them at all today because I'm very restricted on time. Please, Witness, did you join the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I worked in the police, and I was never a member of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you -- what did you do actually?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: After 1992, after the month of April of that year, I continued working in the Republika Srpska police force. I performed regular policing duties. Therefore, within the purview of the police work, and on exceptional occasions we would assist the military when the defence lines came under threat, especially in this area that we have discussed so far. This is where only the villagers resided. There were no additional forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since your house was also there in that area, I am, of course, not mentioning the name of the village, was that the place where you normally stayed, and was that the place where you most frequently took part in the events that involved conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to work from there every day. This is the place where I resided with my family. Very often in my free time when these conflicts were taking place, I would assist and help my relatives and neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that this road was not passable, that you couldn't go from here to the town. Was there any other road that you could use to go into town?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, there was no communication up to the end of August, the beginning of September. You could only go on foot through some hills. Then a road was constructed. Actually, it was a macadam road leading towards Vogosca and also leading towards Mount Romanija and further on towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you look at the photo, could you please show us where this road led in respect of the hilltops that are featured in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The photo is very clear to me. It was taken from the area in front of the barracks, i.e., from the cemetery at Zmajevac. Behind this line, the horizon line, if I may call it that, behind that hill there was this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you more questions about this photo, could you please tell us what you especially did in the Republika Srpska police? Was there any particular job that you would like to mention?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, there were combat activities in the entire area. They intensified. Various sabotage units broke into the area in order to cut off the road. And also the road that connected Pale with another part of Sarajevo called Lukavica, Gojkovici, and Vraca. There were daily incursions aimed at cutting the road in half, and since that was the lifeline for the population that resided in the area, that road had to be defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the road that was constructed behind the hill and the road Vraca-Lukavica, where did this road leave -- lead from -- towards Vraca? It didn't lead towards Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The road that I showed to you behind the hill connected Ilidza, Vogosca, and the settlements over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've already explained that. But the other road, the road leading from Lukavica and Vraca, where did it go?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It went from Jahorina, Mount Jahorina through Vraca and ended in Lukavica across Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you've told us that these roads run behind the road and the one in Zlatiste were under constant threat. Is that what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When it came to the sabotage groups and operations that were very frequent, as a policeman you were involved in that. Do you know anything about Nedzad Ugljen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that he worked in the intelligence service during the war. I read in the press that was under the control of the Muslim media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But as a policeman did you hear of him having anything to do with sabotage operations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That, in my submission, is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please reword your question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the operations that this was -- what is his name, Nedzad Ugljen participated in?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not personally. I don't have any knowledge about that personally, but we did have information during the war that he did participate in the preparation of various sabotage operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now continue. In light of what you have just told us, if we look at this hilltop can you please show us where the positions of the BiH army were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a pen, and can you draw a line from the right-hand side of the screen to the left-hand side of the screen and mark the positions of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a very small-scale photo. I don't know whether I can be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the photo be blown up a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. And now you can do it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put your markings on the photo.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: So I can use the pen to write on the screen? In this forest here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Draw a line along the length, the entire length of --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was at the end of this red line up here where you ended the line? Can you draw a circle there, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you put a letter C next to that circle.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Letter C?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Who was on these positions here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Federation army. The BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where were the positions of the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As you look at the photo from where the photo was taken, they were at a distance of some 40 to 50 metres. Here in this forest or woods there is a facility, a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You misunderstood me. You drew this line depicting the positions of the BH army. Where were the positions of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Behind the hill. I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the hilltop that we see here, where were the positions of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Behind the hilltop at various distances ranging from 15 to 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The line that you have just drawn for us, can you mark it by putting a letter M next to it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the hilltop or the ridge, where would you say that the most frequent conflicts were between the BH army and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I draw that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us a typical place, what would be a typical place. And after having done that, can you also mark that place with a line.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflicts, from the position C you can have a very good view of the road that goes through here leading from Vogosca. From that road every day there was intense shelling, and every day --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark everything that you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see it from this position. You can see it from point C. From point C, you would be able to see the road, not from here where I'm sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And please, I have to hurry up a little. Is there a ridge here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is. I can mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- it says ridge, and it should be cleft. Second of all, the word in the transcript is used as hilltop, and the witness is talking about a ridge and that -- there is a difference, a major difference there. There is a difference between hilltops and the ridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So my question for the witness is this: Could you please draw a line marking this indentation between the hills.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it by putting a letter U next to it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also mark with respect to that indentation where were the positions of the BiH army, and where were the positions of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The trenches of the BiH army were maybe 20 metres from the end of this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, please, follow me closely. With regard to the indentation that you marked, or depression, with regard to that position where were the trenches of the BiH army, and where were the trenches of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The trenches of the VRS were behind the ridge, behind the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark that above the ridge.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This line is some 20 metres behind the ridge, and you can't see it from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you drew the line on top of that ridge?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that what you told me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you put a letter G next to that line, and -- and put "30 metres" to record what you've just told us. Is it then correct that what you've just marked now and what you've just told us that the trenches were some 30 metres behind this line?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, actually the witness has said 20 metres behind the ridge. Just for the sake of clarity and proper recording of evidence. On page 111: "This line is some 20 metres behind the ridge, and you can't see it from here."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us ask the witness to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say? How many metres?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said between 20 and 40 to 50 metres. In this part up to 50 even.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please write down from 20 to 40. From 20 -- write down from 20 to 40 M. At this place where it's 30 metres, you can then add "20 to 40 metres."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Judges, this ridge that stretches the way you have marked it, were there anyone's positions there along this ridge?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the ridge itself, it was not possible to have any positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Because it's a clearing and can be seen from either side. And in war conditions, it would not be possible to stand there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a tower or anything -- you can see on the hill that there is a tower. Was there anything there during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of this tower here next to the point marked with the letter C? That tower was not there during the war, and from what I can recall, it was built in 2000, sometime. From the tower to the point marked with the letter C during the war were the trenches of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from that point how much is visible? Which directions can you see in?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a dominant point, and you can see most of the road that goes from here to Vogosca; and in one part, viewing from my direction towards the right, you can see the other part of the road that leads to -- actually, that was used as a kind of detour during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you please tell us when the clashes occurred? Why did they break out? And you already talked about this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the reason for the clashes in this sector was taking control of the road, because that was a connection with Pale and Vogosca from this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, a little bit earlier you mentioned this tower, Kula. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The small tower was where the army of Republika Srpska was. It was frequently exposed to attacks and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many metres away from the ridge was this small tower?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't be specific about that. You cannot really see it from this angle. I think it was some 20 to 30 metres back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now since I really do have to hurry --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: And from the point marked C, it was some 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic assumed the duty of the commander of the Main Staff -- or, rather, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he assumed that duty in August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident or an event in September? Do you recall that something happened in September there where your house was, where you lived, and when you were at home?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that attack very well. It went on for a long time. It began, I think, around noon. The Muslim forces attacked from all available weaponry with a lot of troops. Many people on our side were killed or wounded. I think they captured some of the positions. I remember I was at home at the time, and I had gone home to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please save this photograph just the way it is as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: With respect, I object to the admission of this photograph in evidence and the markings on it. The -- the witness has given evidence that he was -- he assisted the SRK occasionally. There has been no evidence as to how often that was, when that was. The witness was a police officer in a village which -- which is in a different location. I accept within the vicinity of this location; however, the detailed knowledge with respect to the -- to the front lines, to the alleged front lines, to the positions of the ABiH on the other side, on the enemy's side, requires, in my submission, some further explanation from the witness as it to how he knows this information. How often did he participate? I know I could ask these questions in cross-examination, but I felt that it arose because of the -- the submission to tender this photograph with the marks into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. Witness, you heard the objection raised by the trial attorney, and I would like to echo this question. Can you tell us how you were in a position to provide us with all this information in view of the fact that you only were there occasionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These positions were there throughout the war. They did not change. Who saw them once, knew them as they were, and I saw them whenever I took part in the defence of this sector of territory. These positions are clearly visible from the other side of town, from Vraca, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very quickly, Mr. Tapuskovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the objection by my learned friend Mr. Sachdeva is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you stayed and rested at home every time you came back from the trenches, can you please tell us how many times did these events occur each time you went to positions to help the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The evidence can be now tendered into evidence. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic. Looking at the clock, I can see the 30-minute speaking time we've agreed on are nearly exhausted. You've got another five minutes. So please do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to tender these two documents -- well, rather, this one has been tendered. I wanted to show it to the witness and I had a second which I wanted to explain. Your Honour, Judge Mindua --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go on, please go on .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's impossible to work like this. I'm spending my time. Perhaps I can spend this time at some other place. Maybe I can sacrifice some other witness, but I really need to use this time fully. Perhaps I can abandon using a few other witnesses, but this is a witness that is very important for the Defence. I respect the expenses, the cost, if necessary. I don't know what I need to do in order to have this witness examined the way he should be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, can you look at document D156. Can you please look at the heading of the document, the date, and then what pertains to our forces. You can look at the description of the events there, and you can see whether this corresponds to your description of an event earlier when a lot of people were killed. Can you please read this slowly. The heading, the date, what it is, and then what it states in item 2, entitled "Our Forces." If I can ask you to read aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "At the Sarajevo battlefield our forces on the day," and then it says "army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, commander of the 1st Corps." The date is the 19th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you move straight to the paragraph beginning: "Our forces." The first two paragraphs -- and can you please tell us if this is what you talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Should I read that aloud as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "At the Sarajevo front our forces on the 18th of September, 1994, executed combat actions," combat actions I presume, "In order to occupy Spicasta Stijene and Mala Kula. The following forces were engaged to execute this assignment. One platoon from the 120th Mountain Brigade, Crni Labudovi, the Black Swans, a platoon of the PTOD," I don't know what that means, "of the MUP," of the police,"Bosnia, surveillance and sabotage platoon of the 105th Motorised Brigade, two platoons, two intervention platoons from the 105th Motorised Brigade, a pioneers platoon, an engineers platoon, and two companies in reserve also from the 105th motorised brigade. Upon commencement of the action, the 120th Mountain Brigade captured a sector of Spicasta Stijena, the unit of the PTDO MUP Bosna executed the attack to the right of Spicasta Stijena, and the same upon the commencement of the action destroyed one trench. Further advances were not possible due to continuous fire that dominated in relation to them. By nightfall, the units had occupied a section of Spicasta Stijena and moved the Chetniks back from Mala Kula. During the execution of the attack, the aggressor fired the following weapons: Mortar 60 millimetres, 82 millimetres, 120 millimetres, PAT --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please just look at the last paragraph that talks about something else. Can you please just read that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "The captured part of Spicasta Stijena was held -- or held on or resisted up until the morning hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell us, if this is what you yourself took part in?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is that incident from September when a lot of manpower and weaponry was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see this term, "Spicasta Stijena" being used there repeatedly. You were born there. You are familiar with that area. Was that place ever called by that name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This location, if we're talking about the ridge, which the media during the war called Spicasta Stijena, I don't know why they did that. It was never called Spicasta Stijena. It was called Krs, Bosko Krs, because the owner of the land -- the householder was called Bosko, and I see that term here Spicasta Stijena and I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And what happened with this action of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The attack started around noon with heavy artillery fire at the positions and also the settlement behind the front lines in order to make it impossible for materiel and equipment to be brought in and people to be brought in along the road that leads to Vogosca and the other place east of Pale. And they took control --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me what happen. Were they stopped? What did you do when they were stopped, if they were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were stopped towards the evening. And then during the night we prepared ourselves and returned to our starting positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me what happened in the summer of 1995 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, if you mean the month of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's when an all-out offensive started launched by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at that time, were you faced with a situation in which you took part in an action linked to the area we've just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well, but I don't know if I can give you an exact date now, but anyway, it was around the 20th of June, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us briefly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was an attack once again in the whole area, including a locality -- well, if you look in the direction of the photograph that was on our screen and to the right of that general area, then you will realise that it was an attack on the road, on that communication line. And a lot of men were involved and equipment and materiel, technical equipment, weapons. And I happened to be on the road at the time by chance. I rushed out of my vehicle. I was on my way to work, actually, and I joined the soldiers because I wanted to take shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a document. DD003048 is the number, and I'd like us to do what we did a moment ago. You can look at the heading, the date, although it's a much shorter document. So would you just tell us whether the document reflects the situation you've just described to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unfortunately, we haven't got the translation of this document, but it's a very short document. Just a few sentences if I might be allowed to read it out, and that would complete my cross-examination of this witness -- or, rather, the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I give you leave to read this out, but I remind you that you have used up 45 minutes plus the 20 minutes before the break, so in total 65 minutes. So you are beyond the 50 minutes that I had decided and beyond the 60 minutes which was what we had agreed upon before the hearing. So please do finish up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to read it out quickly then so that I can ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The army of the Republic of BiH." The date is the 26th -- 20th of June, 1995, and it says in point 2.1, it says: "Our forces at 1800 hours launched an attack at the PK LO of the enemy against armoured vehicles and the trenches at Spicasta Stijena were targeted and the trench underneath -- below the crossroads along the Barica-Mrkovici road and Stijene Kula were hit and Krstacka [phoen] Kuca. The effect was excellent. When the trench was targeted underneath the Barica-Mrkovici line the RB mines were not activated. They failed to function." Now, is that what actually happened on the 20th of June 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell me this: Were there any casualties among the soldiers and civilians? And that's my last question to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like this document to be marked for identification until it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Registrar, could you mark it for identification pending the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We'll mark this for identification as D313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you very much. Mr. Sachdeva for the cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness 15. I don't have much time so I'm going to try and do this quickly. My name is Manoj Sachdeva and I'm a lawyer for the Prosecution and I'm going to start now. Let me just try and clarify one thing from you. You went to the trenches, the trenches that you described 20 to 40 metres behind the ridge, you went there every day, is that right, between the period 1993 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say I went there every day, to the trenches every day, but I did pass by the road every day, which is a hundred metres behind this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As to the trenches and communicating trenches, I went there when the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how often did that need arise? How often were you in those trenches every week, per week, from 1993 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The police of Republika Srpska to which I belonged went there some 15 times for seven-day stints to help out as reinforcement, and I went myself 20 times when the fighting was more intense, and I decided to do that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So between the time period of 1993 to 1995, you went to those trenches for roughly 20 times, and you would stay seven days at a time. Is that -- do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, you didn't. I said together with the police when due to an attack in that part of the territory there were a lot of people who had been killed and wounded when the police went as reinforcement to help out, because there were only local people there at the time, very few people, in fact, not enough; that's when we went. Maybe 10 times, but I said that some 20 times I went as a local resident, as somebody who resided in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you said earlier in evidence that there were constant attacks in that area. So I take it there were not constant attacks in that area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that there were constant attacks, and I stand by that. But I had other police affairs to see to, so I couldn't be there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's not correct then that you together -- when you say you went there together with the police when there was an attack, it's not correct that you went there every time there was attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he said quite clearly that a number of times he went to other places with the police, but he said clearly that some 20 times he was there with the locals when there were more intense -- when there was more intense fighting. Then he would help out his locals. That's what he said. So what my colleague Mr. Sachdeva is now putting to the witness is something that the witness did not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva, I can see on page 122, on line 2 that indeed the witness said that he went some 20 times with the local residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll move on. I was just referring to the witness's answer when he said, I went there with the police due to an attack, and therefore I was -- I was trying to understand whether he went there -- I mean, he didn't make a distinction between intense and not intense, but I'll move on. It's not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, let me get something clear. When you went to the trenches, as you said you assisted the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I take it that you were in those trenches with other members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, those soldiers who were also there were under the brigade called the 3rd Sarajevo-Romanija Brigade. Are you prepared to accept that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said I didn't know what brigade it was. I know that it was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. As to the brigade, I don't know which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in those trenches there were roughly 10 to 15 to 20 Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in all the trenches together?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm talking about the trenches behind -- behind the ridge, that the ridge that we have spoken about earlier?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I assume you're talking about those trenches, but do you mean throughout that area, that many people or what.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, when you marked on the photograph the location of trenches 20 to 40 metres behind the ridge? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I recall it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that there were -- well, maybe there were more, but there were at least 25 soldiers there in those trenches during the period of 1993 to 1995 at any one time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There were never that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there were at least 15 then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the regular -- how can I say this? In the regular shifts, there were not even 15. And when there was an attack, then everybody would come in, the elderly and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you were there what weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: An automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What kind of automatic rifle was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: An M-70A type rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also -- at least you and your fellow soldiers also had M-48 rifles, semi-automatic rifles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: M-48, well, there were rifles like that, too, but very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you have -- was there any artillery? Were there mortars within that area? Did you see soldiers with mortars or mortar crew personnel?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In that part, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In which part did you see mortars?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know much about artillery weapons and mortars, but if you're talking about mortars, then that's far behind the lines when you take the road. Some 10 kilometres behind, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So there were mortars positioned in areas such as Gornji Mrkovici and Mrkovici. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May we move into private session just for one second, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So then please be careful, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm guided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I want to show you a photograph. If I could ask for -- if I could ask for 65 ter 03426 to be brought up on the screen, please. Let me ask you one thing, Witness. You said that -- and just so we can agree, you may not have heard it as called Spicasta Stijena, but I'm referring to the ridge as Spicasta Stijena. So you know which ridge I'm talking about, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said to the Court that when Mr. Tapuskovic asked you about who -- who had positions on the ridge, you said no one had positions on the ridge. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this very well. I said on the ridge, and when I say on the ridge, I mean the top line, the top edge of that ridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right. So your evidence is that there was no one on top of the ridge, on that ridge?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not feasible. One could not survive there on the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, during the period 1994 through to 1995, isn't it right that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did indeed have an observation point on that ridge? And as someone who has told the Court, has been there throughout the conflict and has given evidence on very detailed issues, that's something you must know about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what others said in their testimony. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I will get to that in a moment, actually, but firstly, I'm asking you, isn't correct that on the ridge there was a SRK observation point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Even if there had been an observation point, this was not a defence line. I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you were there. You've already told the Court you were at the trenches. I'm asking you whether if you know there was a point on the ridge dug into the rock, roughly 7 to 10 square metres into a hole of 20 by 40 metres. Is that something you know about while you were at the trenches some 20 metres away from the ridge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What witness said it? We should know at least that. I don't remember a witness that said something like that. And if this was indeed said by somebody, could we please at least know who it was who said it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm -- firstly, I'm simply putting the proposition to the witness on a good faith basis, and I will get to the reasons why I'm putting this proposition. I still haven't heard the answer of the witness, and in my submission, what I'm doing is perfectly acceptable. Either the witness can say that he knows nothing of an observation point in the period 1994/1995, or he can give us some more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you again. You told the Court that you periodically went to those trenches some 20 to 30 metres behind, down from the ridge. Now I'm suggesting to you that on the ridge there was a SRK observation point dug into the rock. I'm not asking if you went there, I'm asking if you know about that observation point.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, an observation point should be 20 by 40 metres, and there was no such observation point there, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, whether it's 20 by 40 metres, there was an observation point, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was one, but if those were its dimensions, then I would really be curious to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, let's leave the dimensions aside. Can you please answer the question. Do you know if there was an observation point, no matter how small, on that ridge that was used by the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of such an observation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that the trenches that you were in on occasion, from those trenches there was a communication trench rising up towards the top of the ridge linking up with the observation point? You didn't see that trench either, I take it. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the communication trench that connected the trenches behind the ridge we mentioned, that communication trench did exist, but I didn't see the communication trench linking the trench with the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And those communication trenches went up to the observation point on the top, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. These trenches connected the trenches behind the ridge, and they went 50 metres back in the direction from which the trenches were approached. I'm not even sure that the length was 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, since you served in the trenches, you also know that on the ABiH side there was -- there were some barracks and barracks called Bakije barracks? Is that something you know about? On the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the witness is getting interpretation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you have interpretation? Are you hearing interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. You asked me if there was the so-called Bakir barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Bakije barracks on the ABiH side towards the city of Sarajevo, military barracks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This was the former JNA barracks, and later on it was taken over by the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And -- and that's right. So during the war, during the period 1993 to 1995, the ABiH were in those barracks, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The barracks were in the territory under their control. Whether they actually occupied the premises, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And isn't it right, sir, that the SRK soldiers, the soldiers that you were in the trenches with, would come up to the observation point on -- on the Sharpstone feature and fire down towards those barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for a single moment did the witness confirm the existence of an observation point on that ridge. How many times does one and the same question need to be asked after the witness has answered it once already? How many times does my learned friend expect to receive the same answer? And the answer was that this witness was not aware of an observation point. If I were in my learned friend's position, I'm sure that I would not have been given the same opportunity to ask and re-ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva, indeed you have asked the same question a number of times. The witness has already answered, given you the same answer a number of times. So please try to move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you're aware that in this institution we have had the trial of General Galic. Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, but I don't know whether it was in this particular courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, it was in this institution, but in any case, witnesses -- witnesses for the Defence, for the defence of General Galic, came as you have done today, came here and gave oath -- gave evidence under oath. You accept that that happened, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And one such witness -- well, let me ask you. Do you know someone called Mr. Vaso Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this question goes into the witness's private life. A name is mentioned of a person who was here which directly reveals the identity of this witness. Now we have heard the name of somebody who knows the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness has not yet answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question has been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, my question was perfectly admissible, and it does not in any way identify the witness. I simply asked the witness where he knew -- whether he knew of this person who has testified in open session in the Galic case. And the answer the witness has given is that he knows this person. That does not identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tapuskovic, let's see if we can move on without too many interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've said that you know of -- you know who Vaso Nikolic is. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And he was indeed a soldier with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps during -- during the conflict, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And he also was positioned at the area -- perhaps I'll move into private session just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It would be best to be in private session. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this person that we've spoken about, someone that you know and you've told the Court that you know, came and gave evidence in the Galic case and testified for the Defence. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer? The interpreter didn't quite hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you. I don't have reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when he came here and testified, he testified under oath as you did. That's something you're aware of, that you know that he did that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You've said it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when he was examined, when he was giving evidence, he was asked about the existence of an observation point that we were talking about on the ridge, on the feature that we know as Sharpstone, and I just want to read -- I want to read with -- with the Court's leave, I want to read the questions and answers that he gave to the Court, and then I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I see you standing, but you again would like to object?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am finding it really hard to stand up. I don't want to interrupt my learned friend, but I have to object. First of all, we don't know what period of time are we talking about. Second of all, the testimony that we are going to be dealing with, we have never been warned that this would be used so as to be able to peruse the entire transcript. We are now faced with another delicate problem almost at the very end of these proceedings. We have never received this transcript, and we did not know until a minute ago that this would be used. How can my learned friend now propose to present it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we went through this this morning, and as long as the Prosecution does not intend to tender this earlier testimony into evidence, then it is perfectly legitimate for him to probe the witness by confronting the witness with what another witness has testified. I suggest since we have nine minutes left that you allow the Prosecution to confront the witness here in front of us now with what the earlier witness once has testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to -- I'm going to read the question and answer that he gave under oath to -- to this institution, and as you said, you know -- you know this person to have been a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldier in the same -- you know him to be a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldier. "Q. Could you please describe to us in detail the observation point. How big was it?" His answer: "A. You mean on the sharp rock features? "Q. Yes. "A. Well," -- and the answer is this: "A. Well, that was dug into the ground of the premises of some 7 to 10 square metres. So this was dug into the rock, into the stone, and the only thing you could see, there was just a hole 40 by 20. That was the hole towards the city, an opening." So I'm going to summarise. This person gave evidence under oath that there was an observation point some 7 to 10 metres -- 7 by 10 metres where there was a hole from which one could view the city of Sarajevo. Now, I'm asking you again, does that cause you to reflect on the answer you gave me, or are you still maintaining that there was not an observation point on this feature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I please ask you to observe silence while cross-examination is going on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm waiting for your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not for a single moment did I say that there wasn't one. As far as I know, as far as I went there, I did not see any such thing in that place. If this witness that you have just mentioned said that that was the size, I don't know whether I received a good translation, we are talking about a large-sized place. Ten metres is a lot. I never saw anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, as I said in my earlier questions, let's just -- let me ask you this: Did you ever hear from your fellow soldiers that there was a point on top of the -- on top of the ridge that we see here where one -- where a soldier could look down into the city; in other words up from the trenches where you were? I suggest to you, sir, that you must have heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it is that you're asserting. No, I never heard of it. I never heard of an observation point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is probably as far as we can get on this issue. If you have any other issue, then I think you should move them on so as to allow for Mr. Tapuskovic to have a question or two in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I -- I'm going to, I must admit, find it difficult to conclude my cross-examination in five minutes. This witness has -- at least for the Prosecution there are some critical issues that we have to try and elicit from this witness, and I have -- I did not intend to be -- in fact I was told I had an hour as I was understanding from the 65 ter summaries. I will -- might I just confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva, well, you have no more than 10 minutes. You can go to five minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, before I move on to one further topic or a couple more topics, I'm going to suggest to you that you're not telling the truth about the observation point in this courtroom. I'm suggesting you're not telling the truth about the observation point in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot offer a comment, but I wonder what is it that makes you say that? I have sworn to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. I did not spend four years there as some soldiers did. What I'm saying, I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, sir. When you were there at the trenches, I take that you and your fellow soldiers had binoculars; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have binoculars. Neither did anybody around me. I don't know how important this is for me to say. This locality is actually a forest, and binoculars are of very little use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your evidence is you never saw any one of your fellow soldiers with binoculars during the times you were there at the trenches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: During combat activities, and I would usually be there during those times, it was impossible to use binoculars, and nobody would use binoculars at those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether they were used. I'm asking you whether they were -- whether they existed, whether the soldiers had them. Did they or did they not have them when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know what people had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that -- well, let me ask you this question: You told the Court that you had an M-48, an M-74 rifle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What rifle did you have then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I had an M-78 rifle, and then somebody asked me, I don't know who it was, whether there were any M-48 rifles. I answered that there must have been some, but this is a very old rifle from 1948. A mistake again. My rifle was M-70A, and I would like to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sir, did you while you were at the trenches, did you ever go up to the top of the rock and fire at civilians in Sedrenik? Did you ever do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you repeat the name of the of place?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sedrenik, the village of Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I never went to the top and I never fired at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it while you were there you must have seen some of your fellow soldiers going up to the rock and firing at civilians. Did you see that take place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I must repeat again. During the time when I was in the trenches, when I was on the Defence lines in that locality, this happened exclusively when combat activities were going on. When there was an exchange of fire on the separation line, when there was crossfire. It was impossible to leave the trenches and move in any direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say there was an exchange of fire, I take it you had to be in a position to be able to see enemy soldiers, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you understood me. I don't understand English, so I don't know whether this was recorded. This locality, including the ridge and to the right of the ridge and to the left of the ridge towards other positions is a forest, and it's very difficult to notice anyone. It's very difficult because of the dense fir forest. It's very difficult to see ahead more than 20 or 30 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that during the conflict the trees were damaged and, in fact, many of them were destroyed due to the combat activities? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in certain parts, that's right. There were some trees that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever come to be aware or did you ever hear about SRK soldiers firing from that location where you were, firing at civilians in Sedrenik and into the city of Sarajevo? You must have heard about that, sir, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That soldiers opened fire at civilians in Sedrenik and that part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the BH army? No, never. I never heard about that. And I sincerely doubt that anybody would target civilians. I think that is beyond all reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever shoot any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Had I seen that with my own eyes, no. Now, whether in an exchange of fire or crossfire there was anything like that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Sachdeva. You were very efficient. I congratulate you. So, Mr. Tapuskovic, for redirect, but I now have a little bit of difficulty with the interpreters who are not going to be too happy if this goes on very long, if we go beyond the time foreseen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I went on a little longer last time. All I wanted to do was to deal with this photograph, and I want it back on our screens, and that would have gained time. 65 ter 03426 is the number. It was on our screens just a moment ago, and I just have something to ask regarding that photograph, because I realise that I don't have enough time to go into other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the picture again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on this photograph can you say -- see Mala and Velika Kula, big and small Kula or town?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see it. You can see Mala Kula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, but in my submission this is beyond. This does not arise out of cross-examination. Counsel has shown the witness photographs in his evidence in chief and he could have quite easily have asked the witness to mark certain features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
